speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
After looking into this
amendment carefully, I have decided that it is out of order, as it contemplates a larger expenditure of money than was provided for in the original resolution, which received the assent of His Royal Highness. The amendment reads:
5. Subsection (c) of section 18 of the principal Act is repealed,' and the following substituted therefor:
(c) No judge of a county court shall receive any travelling allowance for courts or chambers held at the county town of the county or union of counties wherein he resides-provided, however, that this subsection shall not apply to any such judge residing at a town (other than the county town) at which the volume of court or chamber work done Is established to the satisfaction of the Minister of Justice to be as great or greater than that done at the county town.

Therefore, for the reason giw^t. I rule this amendment out of order. Uu question is now on the third reading of the Bill.
Will not the Minister of Justice provide, by resolution, for the proposal which His Honour has just ruled out of order?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I might be disposed to do that were it not for the fact that the proposed amendment, which I think ought to be passed, did not seem to meet the wishes of the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte), or of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), I think. If the amendment is not going to remedy the evil complained of, it is hardly worth while resorting to hew procedure to give effect to it.

Hon. J. D. REID (acting Minister of Railways and Canals) moved the second reading of Bill No. 204, to amend the Railway Act. He said :	This this Bill is to renew the
$200,000 per annum to be expended on level crossings. Somebody on the other side of the House has asked me for a statement as to how much has been expended each year. The total amount expended during the five years up to January 1, 1914, is $60,991.22. I will bring down a detailed statement later on. The hon. member for South Renfrew said he was quite willing to let the Bill go through if he had this statement.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into Committee thereon.
On section 1-time extended:
What changes are made by this amendment in the law as it exists at the present time?

There is no change in the
law as it exists. This is simply extending the time for another five years from April 14 of the present year. There is to be no change in so far as the expenditure is concerned.
The provision which was made to assist in the work of the separation of grades expired on the 14th of April?
That is the date.
And this Bill is to make provision for another five years?
That is all.
Is there any change in the amount?

No, the amount remains
exactly the same.
Do I understand that during the past five years only $60,000 was expended?

I called up the accountant
of the commission this morning and asked him to give me a detailed statement of the amount expended each year. He told me that the total amount up to January 1, 1914, was $60,991.22. I thought the amount very small and could not understand how that could be all that was expended during five years, but he assured me that was the total amount expended from the time the Act was first passed. He promised to send me a detailed statement of the amount expended for each year.

I think the
amount is very small. I would have expected a very much larger sum would have been expended. If my hon. friend will give us the information on the third reading, that will be satisfactory.

I would assume that, by reason of the fact that the minister has introduced this Bill to amend the Railway Act, it is not expected that the Bill to revise the Railway Act will be proceeded with at this session. I think it would be wise that it should not be.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It seemed doubtful if
sufficient time remained for taking up the consolidation of the Railway Act and amending Acts, and, as this is a matter that should not be neglected in the meantime, it was thought desirable to introduce this Bill so as to make provision for these crossings in any event.

With reference to the
railway crossings of a city street, under what circumstances, and in what proportion is the cost of making the separation of grades provided for? On whose initiative is the undertaking to he done and afterwards what is the proportion of the cost? I am deeply interested in this matter.

The municipality may make
application to the Railway Commission t-o take the question up and decide whether a level crossing should be eliminated or not. The Railway Commission decide what proportion of the cost the municipality and

the railway shall pay. The Government pay a certain proportion also. The whole matter is entirely in the hands of the Railway Commission.

There are two railways
coming into the city of Edmonton, the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific. I do not think the rights of way actually join, but they are very close together. They cross a number of streets. In providing for the separation of grades, would the two railways be treated as one, or would they have to be dealt with separately? The one work would make a subway under both.

The Railway Commission really have full powers in respect to any city, town, village, or municipal district. Whatever decision the Board of Railway Commissioners may give is law unless it is appealed to the Governor in Council.
Is there any general understanding as to what proportion of the total cost is borne by the two parties?
The Railway Commission decides that.

What is the precedent in the matter? I do not wish to suggest to the city of Edmonton that it make application for subways and overhead crossings, and then have the city stuck for a large proportion of the cost. I rwould like to have some idea as to what the understanding has been in the past, so that we may know what to expect in the future.

I must confess that L am not really well posted with reference to what has been done in the past, but, as far as I can remember, the city makes the application. Of course, the railway may also make application. In that case the city would have to appear and be heard, and it would have to abide by whatever decision the Railway Commission might give. In so far as Edmonton is concerned, if it should appear that a subway would be in the interest of the city, the city would be the one to make the application. I am quite satisfied that the Railway Commission would do what was fair as between the parties.

It seems to me quite evident that either the Act is not what it ought to be, and the municipalities have not taken advantage of it to the extent that they should have done, or
[Mr J. D. Reid.l
there have been more applications than the commission have been able to dispose of; because if, during the five year period which expired on the 14th April last, the expenditure by the Government for the removal of these level crossings has been only $60,000, the amount is absolutely insufficient, and shows that the Act has not been availed of as it should have been. I believe that in the case of Edmonton, the thing to do, as stated by the hon. acting Minister of Railways and Canals, is to apply to the Railway Commission to pass upon the matter. The commission simply orders the work and apportions the cost between the interested parties-in this case the city and the two railways-and the Government comes in with its share. I forget at the moment what is the share supplied by the Government, but my impression is that the Government pay one-third, the railway one-third, and the municipality one-third. It matters not whether the apportionment is made by the statute or by the commission. Though the procedure is easy and summary, the municipalities have not taken advantage of it. Perhaps it is that the commission has not been able to hear as many applications as are made to it. On the third reading my hon. friend should present a statement as to how many applications are now pending before the commission.
I shall be glad to get that information.

The board has almost absolute control over these crossings, and can apportion the cost as between the railway companies and the municipalities, and can also order that a certain sum be paid out of the fund, which is not to exceed in any single instance $5,000. It is rather a surprise to me that the amount expended in five years is only $60,000. My city, on two occasions, made application under this statute, and, speaking from memory, we have received nearly $10,000 to build two subways, which were very expensive structures. The fact that there is so much expense in connection with an over-crossing or an under-crossing deters the ordinary municipality from making application, and the reason some municipalities do not apply is because the aid from the Government is limited. In Toronto they are building a structure over twenty-five streets, and surely the Government's expenditure this year alone will be more than $60,000.

I was very much surprised when the accountant told me over the telephone that the expenditure had only been $60,000. I told him I thought he must mean the expenditure for one year, but he was insistent that it was for the five years.
I shall have a statement prepared in detail as to the expenditure by the Government and by the municipalities, and the number of applications now pending before the board.
Bill reported.

On motion of Hon. J. D. Reid, Bill No. 201, to amend the St. John and Quebec Railway Act, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 2-agreement with Government of New Brunswick and the company:

As I understand this
section, after the expiration of fifteen years the Crown is to receive forty per cent of the earnings of the bridges, worked out on the basis of the cost of the bridges as compared with the total cost of the railroad. Is that the idea?
Yes.
If the bridges cost onefourth or one-sixth of the cost of the road, they would receive forty peT cent of one-fourth or one-sixth of the total earnings.

Whatever the cost of the
bridges may bear to the total cost of the road.

How many bridges
are to be ibuilt and what is the estimated cost?

Three bridges. The estimated cost is a little less than three million dollars, but we put in three 'million dollars to be certain to have sufficient to complete the bridges. Tenders will be advertised for in public competition and the work will be carried out under the Department of Railways and Canals.
Is the minister considering putting in wooden trestles and using train fill?
I do not think so.'

That is only
done on the National Transcontinental.
Is it the idea that the work cannot be started without the consent of the Government of New Brunswick?

When this Bill is passed,
negotiations must be entered into with the provincial Government in order to come to some understanding as to the new agreement that will be necessary. The Government will proceed at as early a date as possible to get matters- into such a shape that they can go on with the erection of the bridges.

I do not know that it
makes very much difference leaving subsection 1 of section 10 as It is, but there is certainly a good deal of verbosity in the subsection. I see that it leaves intact the provisions of the agreement; but, so far as that is concerned, I will -allow the matter to go through, and, if necessary, on the third reading I will bring the matter again to the attention of the- minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We will let the Bill stand for the third reading, and, if necessary, it can be referred hack to the committee. The Bill was gone over pretty carefully by the law clerk of the House, and also by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries; and they assured me, when I looked over the Bill, that it was in proper form.

This legislation seems to be very sweeping, because
practically the whole of the Act is repealed. Now, the Act contains certain provisions which, I believe, in view of what we have heard in regard to section 2 of the Bill, ought to be carefully considered. For instance, rates and tolls are to be considered under se-ct-ion 6 of the Act which reads as follows:
The rates and tolls charged by the bridge company upon or in respect of any of the said bridges so aided shall, before being levied or charged by the bridge company, be first approved of by the Governor in Council.
That seems to be a very wide provision. As I understand it, the bridges are to be built by the Government, and for fifteen years the Government receives nothing. At the -end of that period, they receive a certain proportion of the rates and- tolls charged by the road. Section 6 of the Act provides that the Tates and tolls shall be subject to the approval of the Governor in Council; but according to the Bill now before us, you repeal that section altogether.

We own the bridges now.
,3960
I think it is all right, because the Government own the bridges now.
But the public is interested in knowing what the rates and tolls shall be.
But the bridge company has now power to charge any tolls whatever, because the bridges are taken out of the hands of the company and placed in the hands of the Government.
Are the bridges free?

They will be free for
fifteen years. At the end of fifteen years the Government of Canada will receive whatever their proportion will toe of the forty per cent of gross earnings, because, according to the original scheme, forty per cent of the gross earnings of the railway go to the Government of New Brunswick, out of which the Government pay the interest on the bonds guaranteed under this arrangement. As I understand it, that proportion of the forty per cent which would be the bridge company's proportion comes back to the Government of Canada. The remaining portion of the forty per cent, which would be about five-sixths, goes to the Government of the province of New Brunswick; and, after paying the interest on the bond issue, the 'balance goes back to the St. John and Quebec Railway Company. But our proportion of the forty per cent comes directly to the Government of Canada.
That is exactly it. We have control of the rates.

Section agreed to.
On section 5-commencement of Act:

I must protest against this section. This raises the question that we have been discussing in New Brunswick for three or four years. We want this road built, and we want these bridges built. If section 5 goes through as now proposed, these bridges cannot be touched for a year. The province of New Brunswick is guaranteeing bonds to the extent of $7,000,000, paying it over to a lot of bright, shrewd Yankees in New York, who are using up what little^is necessary to build the road, and are putting the balance into their pockets, or paying it out for political purposes. That railway is of no use without these bridges; and, if section 5 goes through these bridges cannot be touched for a year,

because the legislature of New Brunswick will not meet until say March of next year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Has the legislature prorogued?

Yes, and it simply means deferring this matter for a year. If a bridge across the St. John river is going to cost $2,000,000, it cannot be built in one year, or in two years. If the work is to be postponed for a year, it will take three or four years after that to complete the bridge, so that it will be four or five years before Grand Trunk Pacific business can go into the city of St. John. It is a fact that neither the Government of New Brunswick nor the Government of Canada will be justified in spending a dollar on this road if it is not for the purpose of opening up a highway from the West into the city of St. John. Of course, some money must be spent in building branch lines, tout the idea is to build a through road, and, unless it be a through road, the province of New Brunswick will be bankrupt, because it will have $7,000,000 tied up in one road, and that will be a tremendous financial strain upon the province. Unless this road is so built that it makes a through highway for western business into the city of St. John and gives the people of the province something to do, I do not know what will become of the province. I wish I could make my hon. friends opposite realize the importance of this matter to the province from a financial standpoint. Very serious charges have been made in the provincial legislature regarding the construction of this road. I have made the statement here, and nobody has dared to deny it, that it is not a first-class or a second-class or even a third-class road that is being built. I do not believe it is the intention even to go to Grand Falls. I listened the other day to my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in regard to this matter; and, without cross-examining him, I thought we would have an opportunity of discussing the matter at the committee stage. I understood him to say that, according to Mr. Montserrat's estimate, $3,000,000 would be necessary to build the three bridges-one across the St. John river at or near Andover, one across the St. John river at or near Nistake, and one across the Kennebecasis river at or near Perry Point.
Mr. BORDEN- ^he Minister of Marine and Fisheries has been detained owing to

an important engagement. He is much more familiar with the object of thb legislation than either the acting Minister of Railways and Canals or myself. 1 Therefore, I would suggest to the hon. member for Carleton that we let the Bill remain in Committee until the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is able to be here, and then we can consider my hon. friend's suggestion as to the elimination of this section.

That is satisfactory to
me. The whole gist of the Bill is contained in section 5, because, if this goes through and we cannot commence the building of the bridges for another year, it will be four or five years before they can be completed.
Progress reported.

On motion of Hon. Robert Rogers (Minister of Public Works) the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
Hesolvefl, that it is expedient to provide that the subsidy payable in respect of first-class dry-docks under section 8 of the Dry Docks Subsidies Act, 1910 (1910, chapter 17) be increased from three and one-half per cent to four per cent per annum of the cost of the work as fixed under the Act, during a period not exceeding thirty-five years.
Will the minister please explain this resolution ?

This resolution is presented to meet the difficulties that are found in raising the necessary capital for the construction of a first-class dry-dock. Hon. members will understand that a first-class dry-dock is one that is not less than 1,150 feet in length, with a width of 116 feet and a depth of 37 feet. Under the old Act, the subsidy was based upon an amount equal to three and a half per cent of the cost of such a dry-dock. Section 8 of that Act provided:
The subsidy payable in respect of dry docks which have been constructed under this Act shall be-
(a) if of the first-class, a sum not exceeding three and one-half per cent of the cost of the work, as fixed and determined under subsection 2 of this section, each year during a period not exceeding thirty-five years from the time the Governor in Council has determined, under this Act, that the work has been completed.
Subsection 2 provides:
The cost on which the subsidy shall be calculated shall be fixed and determined by the Governor in Council, upon the recommendation of the minister, based upon the report of the chief engineer of the Department of Public
Works, accompanied by plan,, and specifications of the proposed works, and such cost shall include the cost of all necessary equipment, machinery and plant, and any sum bona fide expended or to be expended by the company in the purchase of a site for the dry-dock, but shall not include the value of any site received or to be received by the company by way of bonus or gift; and the amount of the subsidy shall be so fixed and determined before the agreement for payment of the subsidy is entered into.
In view of the cost of money at the present time it has been found impossible for companies to undertake the construction of a first-class dry-dock on the basis of a subsidy of three and a half per cent, and it is proposed to increase it to four per cent. We have at present .a crying demand from Vancouver for a dry-dock of first-class dimensions, and it is apparently impossible to get any company to undertake the work on a basis of a three and a half per cent subsidy.

I presume that I shall be correct if I understand the minister as saying that this applies to docks for which contracts have been entered into as well as for those to be contracted for in the future ?
No; this applies to the future only; there is nothing retroactive about it.

Does not the hon. minister think it could be extended ? For instance, take the case of the dry-dock at St. John. As he knows, a company is building a dry-dock, and I think I am safe in saying though I have no personal knowledge of the matter, that on account of the financial stringency iabout which we heard so much from the Minister of Finance last evening, they have difficulty in financing on a basis of three and a half per cent for thirty-five years. Would not he feel justified in extending this increased subsidy to the dry-dock at St. John just as though the work were in the future ? It is true, the dry-dock has been commenced and a large amount of work has been done; but it seems to me it would be reasonable and fair, and in the public interest, that this should be made retroactive to cover the case of dry-docks in the course of construction. Let me point out another thing. The dry-dock in St. John, as I understand it, may not come under the head of a first-class dry-dock as the minister has described it or in commercial language. It is only 900 feet long, but they are building in Levis, and I think on the Pacific coast, docks 1,100 feet long. Would it not be reasonable

for the minister to include the St. John dry-dock in this resolution and provide that it be made a first-class modern dry-dock in .every respect ? I hope he will see his way clear to carry out this idea.

The same conditions that apply to St. John would apply to other cases as well-to the case of the Montreal dock, for instance. And I do not see how it would be possible to stop even there. We should have to go back to other docks that have been subsidized under contract made with the Government and with Parliament. In the case of the dry-dock at St. John, we have there a reputable company, as I understand it, that has undertaken to construct a dry-dock and has made a definite and specific contract to carry out that work on the basis of three and one-half per cent. I do not see how it would be possible for me to recommend that we make this legislation retroactive. In the case of the St. John dry-dock, we have offered the contractors who have made a contract on the basis of a dry-dock of 900 feet that whatever amount a dock of 1,100 feet would cost, we will extend the contract on that basis should they desire it. I do not think it would be the part of wisdom to make the legislation retroactive, because as I have said, it would be impossible to stop at the case of St. John, but we should have to include the dock at Montreal and even go back to the beginning of the building of dry-docks. I do not think it would be possible.

I do not think there are as many lions in the path as the hon. minister seems to think. He is looking at this matter through distorted glasses. Not many dry-docks have been constructed under this Act. I do not think there is a first-class dry-dock in Canada, except the floating dock at Montreal. I speak subject to correction. I think the minister would not be violating any principle if he extended the scope of this resolution to include the St. John dry-dock. He says he will agree with the contractors to build a dock of 1,100 feet if they do it on the same basis as that on which they are now building the dock of 900 feet. But these terms are very onerous; the more docks you build on those terms the poorer you are. When you have a bond the interest on which is guaranteed for thirty-five years at three and one-half per cent, you have not a very saleable proposition under present financial conditions. When my hon. friend asks this company to extend their

dock 200 feet under the present conditions, he is only putting them in a position to lose more money.
We did not aisk them to do it.

When the people of St. John asks them to do it and my hon. friend comes back with this offer, it is only asking these people to lose more money than they are doing now. It seems to me that if the minister would make this retroactive so fair 'as the St. John dock is concerned, he would give us in St. John the opportunity of having a really first-class dry-dock 1,100 feet in length, the same as those at Levis, on the Pacific coast, and, I believe, at Halifax. I consider that this is only a reasonable request >amd I still hope that, notwithstanding my horn. friend's rather pronounced views on the subject, he and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will be able to get together and put St. John in the same position as these other great national ports.

The considerations that
would apply to first-class dry-docks would also apply to second-class dry-docks, so that this would have to be done at Port Arthur, Montreal, Prince Rupert, Sault Ste. Marie, Toronto and St. John. But I do not see how it would be possible to carry out such legislation as the hon. member has suggested by reason of the fact that if we adopt any retroactive legislation it would have to be applied to all of these dry-docks.

I quite sympathize with the view taken by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell). I do not know personally of the case at St. John except by rumour and by what is being published in the press. I know that this great dock will revolutionize things at St. John. The effect of the establishment of a floating dry-dock in Montreal by the Vickers firm has certainly been to improve the condition of our whole transportation system. As pioneers in that new industry, the Vickers are certainly entitled to preferential treatment, and I know that they are at present asking the assistance of the Government to recoup them for the very large expenditure which they have made in order to give Montreal and the St. Lawrence the benefit of their dock. Since the establishment of that floating dock many ships which have suffered accident have been repaired in Montreal. Still it has

not yet become a paying institution and I am quite sure that if the Government would apply the present legislation to the few cases which exist, making it retroactive for these few cases, it would be simply doing justice to the pioneers. I would like to put in a good word for the Vickers Company because they have certainly improved considerably the conditions of transportation in the St. Lawrence, and especially in Montreal.

We all appreciate what
the Vickers Company have done in the construction of the dry-dock in Montreal which is giving, as I understand, entire satisfaction. At the same time in view of the fact that a strong company, such as the Vickers, have made a contract foT the construction and operation of this dock,
I do not see how we could fairly ask Parliament to amend the subsidy after the work has been practically completed and give them an advance on the subsidy for which they had already contracted to build the dock. It is true that there was an understanding, implied or otherwise, at the time 12 noon, they made the contract, that ' they were going to have the opportunity of building a navy for my hon. friends opposite in the city of Montreal,. and that, in view of that prospective work, they made a contract for the building of a dry dock at a lower rate than they probably otherwise would have asked. I for one would be very glad, if possible, to amend the Subsidy Act in some way that would lend them assistance, because of the fact that their dock is giving entire satisfaction; but if you do that in the case of Montreal, why not in the case of Prince Rupert or Port Arthur or the Sault or Collingwood? That is the difficulty that confronts us. Otherwise I would be very glad to yield to the recommendation of my hon. friend, but I do not think it would be possible to do so.

The answer of my hon. friend is so far very satisfactory. I wish to say something, however, as to the suggestion thrown out by my hon. friend as regards the proposed Canadian navy. My hon. friend has supplied us with an excellent argument which was combatted by hon. gentlemen opposite when the discussion took place last year, namely that we were in a position to build a navy in Canada. Now, it is perfectly true that when the Vickers established" their
floating dock in Montreal, with their shipyards, they had in mind that, possibly in the near future, they would receive orders for the proposed Canadian navy. They were entitled to expect that, and if it is true that they believed that they would receive such orders. Is it not then, surprising that the Prime Minister last year contended that for fifty years Canada would be unable to build ships? I remember perfectly the circumstances of the establishment of the Vickers shipyard in Montreal. They stated then, and they state today, that if the Government would live up to the expectations which were given in 1910, they would certainly undertake to build, not the dreadnoughts but the smaller cruisers which would be a part of the Canadian navy. I do not wish to start a debate on the Canadian navy, but I am glad to hear my hon. friend confirm the statement made by several members of the Liberal party last year that if Canada wanted a navy our own shipyards could build the vessels.

Perhaps it would not be out of the way for me to recall to hon. gentlemen opposite that what has been said about Montreal is true of St. John to a greater degree, because in the case of St. John there was a tender to build part of those vessels, and it was the lowest tender; and my hon. friends opposite had the deposit in their hands when they came into power, but they returned it. I have no doubt whatever that the promoters of the dry-dock in St. John believed-I happen to know they had very good reason for believing-that a portion of those vessels would be built in St. John. I happen to know, and I think the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the Minister of Public Works know, that Norton, Griffiths and Company were working in conjunction with Cammell, Laird and Company, who were the contractors for me war vessels; and there is no doubt that the Government have obtained a better contract with Norton Griffiths and Company for the construction of the dry-dock and harbour works by reason of that company's expectation of building a portion of those vessels. Norton Griffiths and Company were influenced, no doubt, by a contract which they had with Cammell, Laird and [DOT]Company for the construction of the war vessels. I have some knowledge of this, for I was present when the contract was drawn up between these companies, and I repeat that Norton Griffiths and Company

were largely influenced in tneir tender for tire construction of this dry-dock and harbour works by the fact that they expected to work in conjunction with -Camm-ell, Laird and Company for the construction of a portion of these war vessels. I believe the 'Government to-day has a mu-ch more favourable contract with Norton Griffiths and Company by reason of that expectation, which has not been fulfilled, than they would have got without it. 1 had not intended to refer to this, but as the Minister of Public Works has brought the question up, ll give it as an additional reason why the St. John dry-dock and harbour should be treated as generously as the dry-dock at Levis, at Halifax, and the one on the Pacific coast.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I regret I was not here when this discussion commenced regarding the dry-dock at St. John, for which Norton Griffiths and Company have the contract, as I was attending a meeting of the Marine and Fisheries Committee. The contract at St. John included the dredging of the bay, the construction of certain dry-docks and the breakwater there, and the construction of a dry-dock which is being constructed under the- Dry-Docks Act. Although they are constructing that dry-dock under the Dry-docks Act, in a sense, it is well known to the Public Works Department that Norton Griffiths and Company -would never have entered into a contract for the building of a dry-dock if it had not been linked up with the other work I have mentioned. The contract calls for a dry-dock 950 feet long which, when completed, will be one of the largest in the world. Contracts have since been entered into for dry-docks at Levis, Halifax, and I think in British Columbia for diy-docks 1,100 -feet long, and while the 950 feet dry-dock at St. John will probably meet all the requirements for a number of years to come, it might ibe wiser to make arrangements with Norton Griffiths and Company to extend it to 1,100 feet.
That is what I am asking for.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is no doubt that Norton Griffiths and Company would not -have entered into a contract for the construction of the dry-dock unless there had been linked up with it this other work, and all those who tendered for the other work knew that one of the conditions to be complied with was that they were also to construct a dry-dock at St. John under -the provisions of the Dry-Docks Act. Conse-

quently, when they were making up their estimate for dredging, -building a harbour and piers, they had to take into consideration the fact that they were also required to build a dry-dock under the provisions of the Dry-Docks Act,
My hon. -friend -has said that if the Norton Griffiths Company had -got the contract for building certain cruisers and destroyers they would have been built at St. John, but we have the statement of his leader that "if the Government had proceeded with that policy those cruisers and destroyers would at the present time have been under construction at the city of Montreal.
Only a portion of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My right hon. friend made no exceptions. As a matter of fact, it has always been claimed by the representatives of the Canadian Vickers that they have assurances that the work will be given to them when they have completed their floating dock and shipyards at the -city of Montreal.

On motion of Hon. W. J. Roche (Minister of the Interior), Bill No. 200, to amend the Yukon Placer Mining Act, was read the second time and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in the chair.
On section 1

owners of adjoining claims concentrating work on one or more claims,- s. 51 amended to facilitate such agreements between individual miners:

I explained' when I introduced this Bill that it is intended to amend section 51 of the Placer Mining Act. Section 51 as it now stands provides that any number of claims owned by one individual company, or a group of individuals included in any registered partnership, may be grouped for operation, but it does not provide for any group of individuals who have not formed a registered partnership. This



amendment goes farther so as to enable a group of individuals to operate a number of claims by signing a document and producing it before the gold commissioner in which they assume severally and1 jointly all liabilities in so far as the operation of these particular claims is concerned but not in regard to such other things as a registered partnership would entail.

Why do you dispense with some of the conditions which usually occur in a regular partnership? It seems that you are providing for some kind of a legal holding entirely apart from thoste relations which are recognized as existing in a partnership.

It was found that when the Act was put in operation it did not carry out the spirit of the law as it was intended. It gave certain privileges to large operators which were denied, under the construction of the Act, to the smaller operators and this clause is to remedy that apparent defect. In reading the original clause it is not easy to see where the difficulty occurs but it does occur under the ruling that the officers administering the law gave it in the Yukon. This clause has been drafted to remedy that difficulty.

What is the legal
relation to each other and what is the provision in regard to the creditors of the parties who have a holding of this kind?

The legal relation in regard to these gentlemen who combine to group their claims under this proposed legislation coniines their liability simply to the operation of these particular claims and does not proceed beyond that. It is a simple method of making it possible for small individual operators to group their claims in order to do the representation work. The law demands that $200 worth of work shall be done on each claim. This work is known as representation work and this clause is to make it possible for the individual owners to group their claims. If there are ten or eleven claims in one group, all that is necessary is to do $200 worth of work for each claim on one claim. The liability extends simply to the claims concerned owned by each group of miners.

Would the effect be that with parties associated together in this way these holdings would only be liable to the extent of the interest of these parties in this property? Supposing the case of a creditor against the partnership for goods purchased or a case where a party had been

injured-would he need to realize his claim out of that particular holding and would he be unable to proceed against them to recover out of any other property they might hold?
That is the point.
Why has this exception been applied to the Yukon?

The idea is to confine the liability of these operators and to make an easy form of partnership which they can enter into for the representation work on these individual claims, and it was not thought desirable to extend the liability beyond that particular thing.

If a party of miners
group their claims and the assessment work that is contemplated on one claim is not fully done, what happens? Do all the members of the group lose their rights or is there an apportionment of responsibility so that only those who did not contribute lose their rights?

They are jointly and severally liable for the amount of work required to represent the group, and as this legislation is framed especially to meet their wishes, I fancy it would be incumbent upon each individual to satisfy himself that the necessary amount of work on the whole group was performed.
In case the mining inspector gave a decision that the work had not been performed, would all the claims concerned in that group be thereby forfeited?

If the necessary
amount of work was not done, the effect would be that the claims combined in that partnership would be subject to forfeiture. There is, however, a clause by which the original owners may, by doing certain things, get their claims back if through a technical error they place themselves in a position where they might lose their claims.

It would be well while
the Bill is in Committee to have that point definitely settled and the minister might make a clear statement as to it. Would the whole claim be liable to forfeiture and what conditions would surround the recovery of rights.

The latter portion of section 2, referring to the partnership, reads:

Such agreement shall state the address within the Yukon territory at which the notice of cancellation, hereinafter referred to, may be served upon the said partnership; service of such notice at which address shall be good and sufficient notice to all parties to said partnership agreement and to all persons interested. Such permission, however, shall be subject to cancellation at any time by the gold commissioner, with the approval of the commissioner, after sixty days' notice to the persons interested, in case it appears from the report of the mining inspector or otherwise that the system of mining contemplated when such permission was granted is not being installed or operated with reasonable diligence.
I would gather from this clause that it would be subject to cancellation, if the operation of this particular group of claims is not pursued with reasonable diligence.

The department takes
supervision of the work, and if it is not going forward, ultimately forfeiture would result. But under mining conditions, where property is valuable, the law is made plain so that everybody can understand and satisfy himself whether the requirements of the law are being fulfilled. Then, it is a thoroughly understood principle of the administration of the mining law that if the requirements have not been fulfilled by ' A ' the property becomes available to ' B,' and ' B ' forthwith insists upon his rights. If the minister says that on the failure of the joint representation work to be completed within the time and to the amount required by law, all the claims are forfeited and the rights of other men may be asserted in regard to these claims, that is a perfectly clear statement, and we understand exactly where we are. I may point out that it is rather a serious situation, and that it detracts somewhat from the advantage of the grouping, if a man who enters into a group is liable to lose his claim through no fault of his own and without his knowledge of the conditions that render him liable. As long as the law is understood by all parties, that is really the main thing, and after all it is not so much what is said in legislation as what is done in administration. It is not so much what the law says, as it is what the officer of the department says it says, that counts.

That is
exactly the point. My hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) was Minister of the Interior when the law was first made, and it was thought to represent exactly what we in the Yukon intended, but when it was administered in the Yukon this defect cropped up and this 2501
legislation is to remedy it. There is a process of law whereby each of these individual owners shall be notified' and have an opportunity of proving that the total representation work required by the section shall have been performed before their rights will 'be cancelled.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed. *

Consideration of the proposed motion of Mr. Borden that the House go into Committee to consider certain resolutions respecting the Canadian Northern railway, and the amendment of Mr. Macdonald thereto, resumed from Monday, May 18.

Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding
the enthusiastic reception accorded me by my fellow members when I arose, I do not intend to go into this matter at any length. I would like, however, to say a few words upon what might be called the more general features of this question. The problem that presents itself at the present juncture to this Parliament and to the people of Canada is one not only fraught with very serious difficulty, but, with the natural fruition of errors committed in the past, which are gradually developing and coming to the surface, and which in course of time have been dealt with and dismissed from the public mind.
The whole system of Government, like the solar system, is proceeding towards the polar star of control. Hereafter there will be no .such record on the part of the people of this country as there has been in the past of handing over the natural resources and the hard-earned savings of the people to financial buccaneers of any type whatever, that choose to foist themselves upon the Canadian people. One of the great privileges of belonging to the Conservative party and of serving under the distinguished Prime Minister of the present day is that of being able, nay, of being invited to express one's opinions freely. The only necessary qualification known in conservatism is that people shall speak their opinions with sincerity, having given the matter in question some thought, and with a sincere desire to serve the state. It was therefore with pleasure that we all- listened to the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) and the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle). These gentlemen have given

the very best that was in them to the service of the State, and they are thanked accordingly by the people and by this House. There can be no question that they have given a vast deal of thought to this question and that they have done admirably in that service. I am sure, whilst they may not be able tq see eye to eye with us all, nevertheless, realizing the necessities of the situation and having made their protest, they will agree that in order to fulfil the purposes of party Government, it is necessary to fall in line at some time or other.
It is not by any means an admirable thing that an opposition oir any other body of men should have so few ideas that they can be all knocked together in a few minutes and dismissed as casually. It would be better for the Opposition, I fancy, if they differed more om this question, so vital to the interest of the country. Then we would have something worth considering in the way of an amendment instead of one simply to give the matter a six months' hoist. It must surely be a very severe criticism upon the functions of an opposition that, after having debated this question for nearly a week, the only way they can see out of the difficulty is to give it a boost into eternity. That I am sure will not commend itself to the people of the country who admire a brave opposition rather than a cowardly one.
Some horn. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.

When I say ' cowardly I do not mean that they funk the job; I mean that, instead of setting their face one way, they have set it in another and an unusual way. But the people of the country, however, think, as I know the Government know iand we all realize, that Mackenzie and Mann have been allowed too much rope, and that there was very great danger at one time that they would be allowed a little more for the express purpose of hanging themselves with it, if necessary, and there would have been no general regret had they done so.
As the distinguished Prime Minister said on one occasion, the Government were not sent here by the people for the purpose of sidestepping their difficulties; they were sent here by the people for the purpose of transacting the business of the people, and therefore they must boldly face the problem and boldly solve it. They have unquestionably done their best; and while I presume they do not think that their best may necessarily be perfect, yet it lack? amendment.

on the part of the Opp( sition, and we can at least lay that flattering unction to our souls. We may safely say that the people have got tired of being deprived of their just rights, of being made to pay the piper. They no longer intend to do any such thing; and I venture to say that, if Mackenzie and Mann or the Canadian Northern come back here next year seeking anything further, if they are not given the foreclosure but are given any further assistance, there will be not a riot but a revolution' in this country.
It is coming.

Yes, it is coming, but it will take a long time if you give this matter a six months' hoist.
But this is thoroughly realized by the Conservative party; and, apart altogether from the other financial considerations such as the great stringency of the financial world, we must consider the question directly and immediately at issue. That question is whether or not, by a little successful financing, which will not in any way injure others or ourselves to any appreciable extent, we shall be able to tide this great undertaking over a serious difficulty and place the Canadian Northern Railway Company, not for their benefit but for ours, upon a sound footing. That is the question before us; and I am sure it is fit-ing for us to give it our serious consideration and to hasten to give the aid if possible, and we are so doing. It is, of course, gratifying to hear plenty of criticism. It is only in that way that the general knowledge of the country and of the opponents and critics of the resolution can possibly be made use of by the Government. That is desirable; and since we now know that the only thing that can be urged against this resolution is that it had better be postponed, we are thoroughly well satisfied to go on with it without delay. The people of this country, I fancy, do think in that way. They are absolutely tired of grafters, of being made use of, of being made hewers of wood and drawers of water for financial giants, men who, having acquired the distinction and the fortune which they have, put handles to their names in order to distinguish themselves from the common multitude. Are those titles put into this resolution? Are they a security? I fancy not, because they do not furnish any security. They do not indicate the facts of the case, and therefore never should have been bestowed. I say, however, that in view of the fact

that this great undertaking is at stake; that this great difficulty must be faced, the general proposition of aiding and assisting at this juncture is admitted. The right	hon.	leader of the	Opposition,	-with	that	patriotism which
characterizes him, has himself said that aid should be given. Therefore the rest is merely a matter of detail. That is something for the lawyers to settle, or for those upon whom rests the responsibility of furnishing a measure which will escape the criticism of the judges-and if they do that, they will accomplish more than anybody else has ever accomplished yet. But that is a matter of detail and is not germane to the question that is now before us. We are, and have been, discussing the principle of the Bill, and that principle has been endorsed from the first, the criticism that has been hurled at it by a large number of speakers being based upon an entire misconception. The principle of the Bill has been endorsed even by the leader of the Opposition. Criticism of the principle from that or by the hon. gentleman's followers is entirely unwarranted-let these hon. gentlemen dispute with their own leader and not with this Government. They have endorsed the principle. Very well, then, let us hasten the introduction of the Bill and the discussion of the details, and then let them fight about the details as much as they like. But the fact is, we must help the Canadian Northern railway system out of the difficulty in which it is-we must do that for our own benefit; no one denies that. So, let us get out of this quarrel, let us be done with this furnishing of items for the newspapers and material for tremendous headlines. If there be a man in this House who does not endorse the principle, let him stand up and say: Not a dollar shall be spent to give this enterprise assistance. There is not a man in this House who will rise and say any such thing. We simply must decide whether we shall go into public ownership or whether we shall assist this enterprise at this juncture. I think it must be admitted that it is for us to accept the statement of those who are most intimately connected with the management of our finances; and that statement is that however desirable it might be for us to acquire this whole system-and very likely that may be proper in the future when we are in a position to do	it-yet we are
not able to do it now for the reason that we have too much else on
hand. What else can we do except take the word of those who are managing our finances and ibow to their judgment? Undoubtedly the time will come when we shall own all great public works, all means of transportation and communication; and possibly all means of production; and so, instead of having a system of free trade by which people can rush in and grab what they like leaving the rest to take what they have left, we shall have established and demonstrated the true function of government, the public control for the benefit of the people of all the country's resources. Therefore, I say that we ought to get out of the slough of despond In which we are at the present time. Canadians are not the people to lose their nerve in face of impending catastrophe. I admit, and admit readily, that Mackenzie and Mann ought to put every dollar they have into this enterprise and that if we could we ought to compel them to do it, and fight it on this principle. But now the only thing we can say is: Who allowed these men to start out on this voyage of discovery? Which has got us into this difficulty? Who allowed these .men to bind down the provinces, and then having got them tied down, having got them firmly anchored for their own purposes, simply to laugh at us and say: Help us out of the difficulty or else you and yours will meet with misfortune. Who did that? The person who did that, the person who set them on their way, is the person who is guilty of bringing about this catastrophe without the least doubt. The difficulty could never have arisen if it had not been for the fact that the man-or woman-

Oh, oh.
Mr. BURNHAM-who started this enterprise, must have been exceedingly stupid not to have foreseen that financial men, or indeed, the common run of humanity would sooner or later get them into serious difficulty. Now, are any hon. gentlemen prepared to say that British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and the other provinces shall be thrown like bones to the dogs? Are we not to rescue them if possible by using our financial ability, and if necessary our resources? Unquestionably. Therefore, I am sure I am speaking for the larger number of the people when I say: Get over this political bickering and discuss the principle whether we shall save our own credit and our own selves by helping this undertaking. If we should not do so, then let us tell these people to go hence and settle their difficulties among themselves. They have not done the chivalrous thing, and

the decent thing of putting their own property into this enterprise by way ot security. But let us aid them nevertheless, and then when the time comes we can foreclose and put the screws on them all the harder, for the reason that they deserve no mercy.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think I can be charged with unfairness towards the few hon. gentlemen who have spoken in support of the proposed resolutions, without even excepting the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Burnham), if I say that they have failed to meet the precise and peremptory objections raised by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House.
I am free to admit that their task is an unsavory one and that the Government's policy on this question cannot be defended before the country with any chance of success.
Since the opening of this debate, a question occurred to me as it must have occurred to every hon. gentleman who occupied seats in this House last year: How comes it that we should be just now confronted with this contract-making business? During the session of 1913, the owners of the Canadian Northern stoutly assured the Government that their railway system would be carried to completion by them, once for all, if only the country assisted them with a further grant of $15,000,000. They even bound themselves to it. That assurance and that agreement were laid before us toy the right hon. Prime Minister and the hon. Finance Minister, and the Government assumed before the public the whole responsibility under the circumstances.
As regards ourselves, we did not have much faith in that statement, and we refused to ratify that extravagant gift of $15,000,000 to Mackenzie and Mann; but the Government did not stop at that, and the majority in this House passed the Government resolutions, on the guarantee given by the Prime Minister that it was the last grant of public funds which was to go to the Canadian Northern.
To-day that $15,000,000 has been swallowed up, expended, we know not how or where. No satisfactory explanation has been forthcoming, and the Government does not seem to have exercised any supervision over the expenditure of such a large amount of pub-
[Mr. Bumham.J
lie moneys. It seems to me that the primary duty of the Government was to watch over the use which was being made of our moneys, so as to protect the public. Nothing of the sort has been done. Previous to granting this $15,000,000 no inquiry was made into the busines of the Canadian Northern; the Government admit themselves that they have gone into it blindfolded, they allowed themselves to be fooled like children by the magnates of that railway company, and the Prime Minister has made himself sponsor that this $15,000,000 application was final. Then they took no steps whatever towards supervising and checking the use to which this money was put.
I say that under the circumstances, in view of the further legislation which is being submitted to the consideration of the House, such a line of action makes of them, not only the victims, but also the accomplices of the false representations made last year by Mackenzie and Mann to the Dominion Parliament. These same financiers come back a year later and apply to parliament for a further grant of $45,000,000; the country will not permit that its administrators should so complacently let themselves be guided by the men who have just deceived them. In spite of the heaps of figures brought forward-and two of the Government's supporters have shown that those figures are fanciful, and in many cases false-in spite of the efforts made to turn this into a purely technical question, nothing will prevent us from showing it in its true light, and viewing it from the standpoint of public and political honesty.
Before binding us irretrievably to such a gigantic enterprise, before entering into further agreements with the Canadian Northern Company, the Government is in duty bound to require full explanations and a clear statement of the liabilities.
The only measure that might satisfy pubj lie opinion and justify the granting of assistance on the part of the Government, would be, to start with, a thorough and searching inquiry into the business of that company. Such an inquiry is what we demand, what the country demands, and the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) is not the only one in the ranks of the Conservative party who is clamouring for it.
But we are told this is a case of emergency. Under this Government there always exists an emergency. Last year, had it not been for the immediate granting of

535,000,000 to the British Admiralty, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland was threatened with utter destruction. Already in the distance one could hear the roaring of the enemy's guns; the Empire was in a sad plight. This year it is the credit of Canada and the nation's financial standing which are at stake; bankruptcy is staring us in the face, and the only way out of the difficulty is the granting of $45,000,000 to Mackenzie and Mann.
Such an argument is not far from being an attempt at blackmail. If it is to be understood that in this country promoters can with impunity spend right and left the moneys of governments and municipalities, handle and invest for their own personal profit, the funds which are put in their hands for the purpose of ensuring the success of some great public undertaking; and if it is understood, besides, that after managing things in such a way as to bring the whole undertaking on the verge of bankruptcy, they can come (back to the Government and say: Unless you give us more money, we will have to assign and there will result for you a still more grievous situation, I say that is encouraging the improper use of public funds as well as reckless financing.
Before entering into any such arrangement with the Canadian Northern, let us do what travellers over some portions of that route are, it seems, obliged to do: Let us clear the road. And to start with, let us do away with the originators of the disaster, let us get rid of Mackenzie and Mann.
Sir Wm. Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann are two strong men, wizards of finance. They have succeeded in launching and organizing with public funds, a great undertaking, and in surrounding themselves with subsidiary ventures of all kinds. The small company which originated in the province o;f Manitoba and was a long time at constructing a few miles of railway has become a powerful corporation, with twenty-eight subsidiary companies. They have established a system which is well connected and spreads over the whole country. They have taken advantage of that system to develop all the resources which the country puts at their disposal. They have laid hands on everything worth having. They have meddled in politics, they have purchased newspapers. Nay it is rumoured that they were consulted in the making up of the cabinet. They are most certainly great handlers of money and great handlers of men; but I object to letting them continue doing that with the help of public funds.
