And it is after drawing on the public to the incredible extent I have just mentioned, it is after giving a year ago the formal assurance that those $15,000,000 they were receiving would be the last they would call on the country to grant them, that those two financiers now beg for a further advance of $45,000,000.
I admire the candour, or rather the impudence of those magnates. It appears in full light in the letter written by Sir Wm. Mackenzie to the right hon. Prime Minister on the date of March 5, 1914, a letter which is to be found at page 5 of the blue book distributed by the Government.
Ottawa, March 5, 1914.
To the Right Honourable
R. L. Borden,
Premier of Canada.
Dear Sir,-For the reasons mentioned in the memoranda and statements respecting the Canadian Northern Railway System, submitted, it is essential that the company should receive further Government aid. The amount required is forty-two million dollars ($42,000,000).

Recognizing: the difficulties in the way of a cash loan, I beg to apply for a guarantee of securities to the extent of forty-five million dollars ($45,000,000), par value. The discount on the disposal of these securities would probably reduce the proceeds below the forty-two million dollars ($42,000,000).
I have the honour to be,
Your obedient servant
Wm. Mackenzie,
President.
Is not that a simple way of settling matters? For Mackenzie and Mann, this Government is like the Kingdom of Heaven: Ask and thou shalt receive.
It seems to me the Government's first answer ought to have been: Gentlemen you are worth several millions, you have money invested in all sorts of profitable ventures in this country and abroad. Show as much disinterestedness and as much confidence in your undertaking as Donald Smith, Stephens and the other great builders of the Canadian Pacific railway. Before calling on us for further contributions, invest some of your own money.
That is not what the Government say. On the contrary they submit a measure involving the credit of Canada for a further amount of 845,000,000 in favour of Mackenzie and Mann, and binding forever the country, by holding it responsible for the future liabilities of the company and putting us under the necessity of advancing further amounts which will be required for the completion of the road, whatever that may be.
All the securities which the Canadian Northern is supposed to give us are worthless. Before they could be converted to any use, we would have to pay off the $312,000,000 of liabilities which are a lien on all the assets of the various companies subsidiary to the Canadian Northern. The stock which is handed over to us is not worth a single cent on the money market. And by accepting that stock, we enter into partnership with Mackenzie and Mann, in a company whose managers and directors they are.
I say that besides incurring immense liabilities, the Government endorses a wrong principle iby making the Government enter as a partner in a private undertaking. The State should not be a party to any private venture; it should regulate, control, and supervise all of them.
Neither do I approve the appointment of a representative of the Government on the board of management of the Canadian Northern. That privilege is quite useless as an adjunct to the controlling power

which is vested in the State; such a representative will only act as a connecting link between politics and finance, and that, with reference to negotiations which may not always be in the public interest. In the management of the affairs of the company, that director will be a nonentity; his power will be of no avail 'whatever.
Mr. Speaker, the legislation which is submitted to us strikes me as pernicious and contrary to the public interest. If Mackenzie and Mann are unable to meet their liabilities and to build the Canadian Northern, if the country is to pay the cost of that undertaking, let these financiers relinquish their control and hand over the property to the people of Canada.
I, for one, speaking on behalf of my constituents, object to our becoming the subordinates of Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, and I shall vote against the resolutions submitted by the Government.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to address the House briefly on this important question, which is a business question and should therefore be approached and dealt with in a business spirit. It appears to me that Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann started out to build a transcontinental railway with public money. They have got all the money they could from all sources but the road is not yet completed and they have come back to this Government and asked for more assistance. It is our first duty to look carefully into the matter and .see how the money that has been committed to their charge for expenditure in this enterprise has been expended. In order to do that it will be necessary to examine their books not for one or two years but from the inception of the enterprise, about 1896. From that time until the present they have been constructing branches and roads with public money. It would be necessary to examine thoroughly not only their books but also the quality and character of the construction work on the different roads. A short time ago this Government appointed a commission to examine with care into the construction and expenditure of money on the Grand Trunk Pacific. That commission examined very carefully not only the books but every feature of the road, every piece of rock-cut and trestle work to see the quality of the work and the classification that had been made. It would have been quite in order to have done the same thing in this case, and I do not think that this Government have looked into the question as fully as

they should have done. It would have been impossible for them to have done so in the short time that has been at their disposal. The very formation of so many different companies controlled by two men would look to me suspicious. It would look as though there might be some room for sidestepping. One of the first necessary steps would have been a thorough examination of all of these matters. Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann are practically the owners of the Canadian Northern railway, and whenever they undertook to build either the whole line or a branch they first got their charter, then they got all the aid they could from all sources, municipal, local Government and Dominion Government, and then, after making their financial arrangements, they let the work to a construction company which was still Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann. This, to my mind, would indicate that there might be a chance for a little rakeoff. Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann may be a special brand of humanity, more honest than the ordinary run, but the poet, a wiser man than I and one who understood human nature better than any other man of his day or generation, has said:
But, och! mankind are unco weak An' little to be trusted ;
If self the wavering balance shake,
It's rarely right adjusted !
So it appears to me that when Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, owners, let the contract to Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, contractors, without competition, the work to be supervised, examined and looked after by their own engineer, and the classification to be by their engineers, it is very necessary to examine into all these matters with great care and to see if the money that this country has paid from all sources has been legitimately and honestfly texl-pended in the construction of this road. After that examination has taken place if it is found that they have administered the money committed to their charge honestly and fairly, if no misappropriation has been made, and no money has been devoted to other uses, then it -might be well and wise to entrust them with more money o-r credit to finish the- road. If, on the other hand, it is found that a part of the money has been appropriated to outside enterprises, and not to the construction of the road, it would appear to me to be very bad judg-tm-ent and very bad policy on the part of the Government who have trusted them to entrust them with any further public money.
There are in all some 28 or 30 subsidiary companies mentioned in the resolution that has been placed before this House. There is, however, another little organization that is not mentioned. I do not know whether that is organized under letters patent or bow, but in this little organization there is perhaps the most serious question as to the proper method of dealing with this matter, and that is:	if public gossip is
to be relied upon, and if my information is correct, this present Government owes its existence as a government to a large extent to the- influence of Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann in the last election. Not only that, tout if public gossip is to be relied upon and my information is correct, some of the Cabinet ministers owe their seats in the Cabinet to the advice and influence of Mackenzie and Mann. That being the case, it strikes me as though these gentlemen could not approach this question with an unbiased mind and deal with it absolutely on its merits. I would be inclined to think that they might be prejudiced a little: bit; they might feel that they owed a debt' of gratitude or a debt of something to those to whom they owed their positions in the Cabinet; and, while, perhaps, they might intend to be honest and fair, they would be prejudiced. For that reason, when Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann came before this House at t<he opening of this session, I think the wise thing for the Government to have done would have been t-o appoint -a committee selected from both sides of the House t-o investigate this whole matter. The construction of the Canadian Northern railway is a public enterprise, and I think it is agreed on all sides that it is one which cannot be allowed to go to the wall. It must be finished in some shape. But before money is asked for, the first thing that we should know is that the money already granted has been honestly expended. The next thing is tlhat the money we are about to guarantee or grant will be expended honestly without any question. It would be necessary to know the past records of these gentlemen before we entrusted them with further credit. That is how the -matter appears to me. I understand that the Solicitor General drafted this resolution. I do not know to whom he owes his debt of gratitude or his seat in the Cabinet, but evidently not to the hon. member for Calgary.
It was stated in this House during the debate on the Grand Trunk Pacific that the

commission appointed by this Government to investigate the construction of that road came back to this House and reported that the road had been extravagantly built. They reported that it cost a lot of money, but they could not point to a dollar that had not been honestly spent. In this case we find 1100,000,000 of watered stock. I think the wisest thing to do is to cut out all watered stock. I am satisfied that when the road is completed, if it ever is, it will have enough to do to pay interest [DOT]on the actual money expended on the road without having to pay a dividend on watered stock. You may say that we will not have to pay dividends on the water until the bonds are taken care of. That is true, but the owners of the road will say: We have a certain amount of stock on which we have never paid dividends, and consequently we are entitled to charge higher rates; and when the Board of Railway Commissioners is called upon to adjudicate between the public and the road built with their own money; the then holders of this watered stock will point out that on $100,000,000 of stock no dividends have been paid, and from that they will argue that the rates should not be reduced until a dividend has been paid. I say that there should be no watered stock at all. This resolution, as I understand it, proposes to reduce the stock to $100,000,000, but I say there should be no stock at all [DOT]except what represents actual cash. The Minister of Finance, in his speech yesterday, said that this road was a legacy handed down by the late Government. All I can say is that the Minister of Finance is more generous than he was two years ago when, shortly after this Government came to power, he boasted of having a surplus of $39,000,000 and gave the present Government credit for that although they had only been in office about three months. The Minister of Finance did not give credit to the late Government for that legacy, but when he comes to something that is a little knotty-a proposition to which they have granted assistance in two successive years without taking the members of this side of the House into their confidence at all, or giving any reasons, and now, when they come back for the third time claiming to be bankrupt and broke, he says it is a legacy left by the late Government. That is not very logical.
There is just one other point with which I would like to deal and upon which I would like some information. Has any arrange-
ment been made between the Government and Mackenzie and Mann for taking over the Quebec and Saguenay road? My impression is that some arrangement has been made for taking over that road when this assistance is given, and I think we should be given some information on that point.
Before I take my seat, I wish to appeal to the fair and unbiased minds on both sides of the House. While the Canadian Northern cannot be allowed to go into bankruptcy, this House is not justified in putting through any deal or granting any assistance until we know absolutely what these men have done with the money they have received, and how they are going to dispose of the money that is provided for in this resolution. It is absolutely necessary for us to know whether they have legitimately, honestly and faithfully expended the money that they have received from the Governments of this country, Dominion and provincial, or whether it has been put into side enterprises of their own. It seems to me that Mackenzie and Mann must have received a profit or rake-off out of their railway construction. Mackenzie and Mann, if my information is right, started life like myself without any worldly goods, and to-day they are rated as very wealthy men altogether outside of the railway business. I want to know where all their money came from. Did it fall like manna to the children of Israel? If they are millionaires outside of their interest in the Canadian Northern and other railroads, where did their fortunes come from? It is something I cannot understand, and which we should know before we guarantee their securities to the extent of $45,000,000.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment before the House in substance denies that the company is in distress, and therefore denies that it is incumbent on the Government, in the public interest, to come to the succour of the company. I take the proposition before the House as involving that this company, and this great proposition, are in distress, that the Canadian Northern railway needs money to complete its line, and that the Government regard it as a public duty to come to the rescue of the company to prevent what would be substantially a panic. I believe the credit of Canada would be greatly injured if this company and this proposition were allowed to go down at the present time; and if that is the case the amendment does not meet the situation. It proposes to

put oft something that nearly everybody in this House says must be dealt with: the government say so, the majority on this side of the House say so, a great many members on the other side of the House say so, and the last speaker has said so. Therefore, it is incumbent on Parliament to deal with this proposition not only because of the company, but because of the credit of Canada. We could not afford to have the credit of Canada jeopardized, to-day in any way by reason of the collapse of a great transcontinental road that was put into existence by this Parliament, whether by one party or another. This Parliament of Canada is responsible for the fact that we have one great transcontinental road in this country and are building two others on the money and on the credit, principally, of the people of Canada. The Government, apparently seized with that idea, proposes to do something, and they have introduced a measure which will give relief to the company and will, we trust, allow the road to tie completed, and I trust that in the end it will be an advance on what we have done here in the past. To my mind, the proposal before the House is the first step toward public ownership of a transcontinental road in which this Parliament has invested a lot of money. It is true it is not complete public ownership; perhaps it is a partnership; or, as I would prefer to say, by consolidating these companies into one proposition we are putting the system in shape so that in a short time it may be acquired by the people of Canada and linked up with the Intercolonial. We should then have in the hands of the people of Canada, and in the hands of Parliament, a great transcontinental line owned by the people of this country. Having done that, we may go a step farther and complete our own- transportation system by steamships on the ocean.
There is no solution of the transportation problem other than public ownership, and I welcome this as I would welcome any other step in that direction. The only particular in which this proposition does not quite commend itself to me, as an advocate of public ownership, is that when wo take 40 per cent of the stock and assume this responsibility, the least we ought to do is in some way or other to take -an option on the remaining 60 per cent. Now probably is the time to do it. I do not know but that the owners of the road, the Mackenzie and Mann interests, are prepared to entertain such a proposition. It is true it would
cost some .more money, but it would only be fair to take over that interest. I do not say that we ought to do it just to-day but we ought to be able next year, or the year after, to -know how much of an additional cash payment to these owners would give us -complete control of the road. It will be three years before we can get possession of the road in oa-se of default. I do not want to see a default, but I do want to see the road linked up and got together, as it is being got together by this resolution, and I want to see the country get 40 per -cent of the capital stock because that is a substantial approach to public ownership. Next, I would like to see provision made in this resolution whereby we would have an option on the 60 per cent of the capital stock that the proprietors still hold.
I do not believe it would take a very large sum to acquire that ownership. If we do not find the road going as it ought to go, if the money is not put where it ought to be, we would be able to exercise immediate ownership and enter into possession -and we could proceed to do what we must do in any event in a short time; that is-, take control of one and perhaps two of the transcontinental railways. I have been an advocate of public ownership for many yeaTS -and I seek to advance it on every occasion. It may only be a ismall step forward, but I am prepared to support any step in the direction of public ownership. If there is anything that has failed it is the -system of private ownership of- railways wherever it has been tried, whether in the United States, -in Canada, or even the mother country.
Does this proposition secure public ownership?

It establishes forty per cent of public ownership. It goes that far, and this is the first time it has ever gone that far in this country. Private ownership has failed. The present system of railway building has failed. What is the situation in the United States to-day ? The present system has brankrupted most of the great railways because they have been exploited by private individuals and companies and by interests that were not identified with the public. It is abundantly evident that in the United States the big corporation system in relation to railway construction and management has failed. The roads have been exploited, looted, so much money has been taken out of them,

so many unnecessary securities have been put upon them, that they cannot pay their way and they are imploring the country to allow them to increase their rates. I do not think they will get that increase in rates and they will put the railways into the hands of the Government in the interest of the public and try to save something for themselves.
Does the hon. gentleman think that forty per cent is of any use as far as public ownership is concerned ?

It may be. I hope it is. It makes the acquirement of whatever remains much less onerous and it enables us at once to connect up the Intercolonial in the direction of public ownership. It does not go all the way, but I want to see it go the full length, and, either by an immediate settlement with the company for its whole interest, or by an option on that interest, acquire possession of this road. We have in this country at the present time the Transcontinental railway. It is almost ready for use. There is an agreement which sets out that until the whole line is completed the Grand Trunk do not need to take it over. It may be on our hands next year. The Grand Trunk may say: We will take it over under modified terms. Therefore, we may find ourselves with a transcontinental railway on our hands and we may find ourselves with a Canadian Northern railway on our hands. There is a problem coming, and it is one which this Parliament iand the public must get ready to deal with. I am just as surely convinced as that I am standing here that within two years this Parliament and the people of Canada will have to take over the Grand Trunk Pacific-.a transcontinental railway-as well as the Canadian Northern, and link them up with the Intercolonial railway. We may be forced into public ownership, and the consolidation of all these lines in an effort to serve the people and not to serve the exploiters or shareholders.
The great thing in connection with public ownership is that the effort of those in charge of a publicly owned concern is to try and serve the public in the best possible way, to give them the lowest possible rates, not to make a profit and to avoid all unnecessary charges. The conditions that we have in Canada to-day are the result of the system under which we have operated our railways up to the present time. We have an immense and unnecessary duplication of lines and of construction, but compared with unnecessary construction and dupli-

cation, what are the charges for maintenance, the overhead charges, the unnecessary services in connection with these lines once they are constructed? This country will be bled white in maintaining these great transcontinental lines and a lot of unnecessary, duplicated lines and services.
The Grank Trunk, the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian Northern have been telling the people that they cannot stand a reduction in rates. They say that the rates must be kept high, and there is to be no reduction for the farmer or for those who pay the railway rates because of the competition of other lines. Not only have we an unnecessary duplication between Port Arthur and Sudbury and across the Rocky mountains, but we have unnecessary duplications in all directions. It costs a lot of money, and the rates are unnecessarily high in consequence. Therefore, the only real relief, the only possible relief, will be the consolidation of these lines into one system, and the only interest that can consolidate them is that representing the Parliament and people of this country. We have built at an enormous cost' four lines across the mountains. The Canadian Pacific railway are constructing a second line, the Canadian Northern will have a line, and the Grand Trunk Pacific will have one. One double track line between Edmonton and the Pacific coast would be worth all the other lines put together, considering the matter from the point of efficiency and reduction of rates. While we have built these roads, we still have the problem of finding a way of making them profitable. My contention is that the only way is to consolidate them in the one system and have that system controlled by the state. Between Toronto and Ottawa, within the next few weeks, we aTe to have four lines competing for passengers and freight. I believe that one line double tracked would do all that work much better. We have got to wipe out this unnecessary duplication, even if we have to take up the rails of some of them and put them down in other places where they will give better service. To my mind the problem before us is to recover our mistakes, to try to come to public ownership in connection with one or two of those lines, and then to approach the real problem and work out the consolidation, wipe out the unnecessary lines, and try to give good service. We have been trying to build railroads, but we have not been giving the service

we ought to give to the people, and we will never be able to give a proper service with all these competing roads. You cannot do all this in a moment, but you can begin to get ready, and my appeal here to-day is based on the idea that we must begin to get Teady, and this legislation before us i's the first sign I have seen in the history of Parliament that we are getting really ready for the public ownership of our railways, in part if not in whole.
This road came before the attention of Parliament in 1898, when 1 was a member of this House, and I then urged, in connection with the proposal to subsidize the Canadian Northern from Winnipeg to Port Arthur, that it be made a public road. Mr. Robertson, then member for East Toronto, and iMr. Richardson, then Libera! member for Lisgar, urged with me that the road should be nationalized and that it be thrown open to the Intercolonial railway, and had that been done it would later have been open to the Transcontinental railway. But that was not done; we subsidized the Canadian Northern then, and we have been subsidizing it ever since, and the result i'S that we are in a mess. We have now three transcontinental railroads; we do not see how they are going to maintain themselves, but we do see that they are coming back ihere year after year for additional consideration. The Grand Trunk Pacific, I am told, will be back here again for assistance, the Canadian Northern is now asking for assistance, which means that they are to have one hundred million dollars to spend. We do not quite know if that will complete the Canadian Northern railway, and, although we were warned years ago that it was a mistake to unnecessarily duplicate these lines and to spend money on them, we have continued to do so right up to the present hour, and we find ourselves where we are to-day. We must try and recover our ground, we must try and get rid of these unnecessary lines. How it is to be worked out I do not know, but I say it can be worked out if men who do believe in public ownership have the responsibility of doing it. A party is growing up in this country in favour of public ownership, and when we have public ownership we will have the means of regulating transportation charges in an effective way, and we will be in a position to regulate ocean freight rates also. I am ready to-day, on the lines of public ownership, to subsidize or purchase
a line of steamships that will give relief from the exorbitant freight rates that prevail on the Atlantic. Our farmers in the West are not making as much as we expected they would, because they say they are unfairly treated in the matter of ocean and railroad freight rates. And yet we have spent hundreds of millions, a billion of money almost in building railways, and we propose to continue it and to duplicate railway lines unnecessarily, and to pay overhead charges that we ought not have to pay. If we now begin to cure these mistakes of the past, and if we can get one or two of these lines into our hands and use them to that end, we will begin to effect some kind of reform.
The question of public ownership came up when this railway first came to us for aid fifteen years ago. The right hon. gentleman who then led the House said he did not believe in public ownership, and he repeated that statement when the Transcontinental Railway Bill was introduced, but he now shows signs of change of view because he says that we should get all the stock of this railway. If there is a way that we can get it now, even by additional expenditure or by taking an option on it, I think we ought to try and do so. As it is, this measure seems to me to be somewhat in the right direction and it does seem to me to be in the line of upholding the credit of the country and of getting rid of a situation that otherwise will bring discredit on us, will injure our credit, and will impede the settlement of the country generally.
There are some things in connection with this deal I wish to point out. The Minister of Finance said last night that for one thing it meant the limitation of the capital stock of the Canadian Northern railway, and of the subsidiary companies, and it does do that. The minister claims credit for that and I heartily congratulate that gentleman on his conversion, because I have heard ministers of finance and other ministers, and I have heard the law officials of the Government say that it is not necessary to control the capitalization of railways. Now, for the first time we have it on the statute book in connection with one company, and if we have it in connection with one company we must have it in reference to all, and this Parliament ought not to prorogue until it takes control over the capitalization of all railways. The principle is contained in a Bill now before the joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, to regulate the capitalization of

all railways, and there is a rumour that this Bill will not go through this session. If that be so, my advice to the Government is that they should pass a Bill with a single clause in it, taking complete control over the capitalization of the Canadian Pacific railway and all other railways. I have pointed out to this House on several occasions that the increase in the capital stock of the Canadian Pacific railway was against the public interest and that it ought to be controlled. I was voted down time after time, and at one period I could hardly get a seconder for my motion, but now the principle is admitted. What has been the net result of the watering of the stock, or the cutting of melons in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway stock? It has been this: that while they cut melons for the benent of the holders of the Canadian Pacific railway stock and divided $80,000,000 amongst them, the shrinkage of value of the stock since the Canadian Pacific railway began this system of cutting water-melons, has amounted to over $100,000,000. It is foolish any longer to allow these companies to unnecessarily increase their capital. There was a time when the Canadian Pacific railway was capitalized at $50,000,000, and it should have been kept there, and had it been kept there the people of this country would have owned the Canadian Pacific railway. To-day it is capitalized at over $200,000,000, and the stock is owned outside of Canada, and the capitalization is so great that Canadians can never buy control. The capitalization of the Canadian Pacific should have been kept largely to the issue of bonds and debenture stock, and the control should have been in the common stock, which should have been limited. Had it been limited, the people of Canada, as individual investors, would to-day have had the control of it and we would have been in better shape. Therefore it is quite clear that, if we are limiting the stock of the Canadian Northern, as we are doing to-day, we ought to limit the stock of all the railways of this country and not allow them to increase their capital or to water it when they like, so that their stock may be what it has never been yet in this country to any great extent, namely, devoted to the purposes of the undertakings. If this stock of the Canadian Northern railway had been kept in the treasury, it would have been almost sufficient for the needs of the company to-day; but it has been allowed to be taken out of the treasury, and the result is 
that the stock has never played any part in the financing of the railroad. Therefore it is now incumbent upon Parliament to see that all the railroads in Canada are this session put under a general Act, which will compel them to secure the approval of the Railway Board for their financial propositions. That is one good result that has come from this proposed deal with the Canadian Northern railway.
As to whether or not it will be possible for this House at this time to find a way whereby we cam get an option on or can purchase the 60 per cent of these shares, I do not know. The Prime Minister, however, has invited suggestions and this is one I throw out to him, that he should see whether it be not possible to secure at a reasonable price the controlling shares of this railway. Perhaps the owners would object to that; perhaps they have other ends in view; but I would like to see at least negotiations opened up, and not only an effort made now to complete this road and to maintain our credit, but a real, earnest effort made to have the state and the people control at least one transcontinental line. Now that we have started to secure 40 per cent of the stock of one railroad, there must be no further change in the status of the Intercolonial railway, nor must any railroad 'be allowed to get rights over it other than other roads have. While they may have common use of it and running rights over it, its integrity must be maintained absolutely. During the last few years these have been proposals in this House and in the country at various times that the Intercolonial system ought to be allowed to lapse into one of the other roads, or that its usefulness ought to be interfered with by unfriendly agreements, tie-ups and things of that kind. We have to maintain the integrity of the Intercolonial. We are to have 40 per cent of the stock of one transcontinental road. We should try to get the rest of the stock of that road. Whether we will or not, we have to get ready to deal with the National Transcontinental system or the Grand Trunk Pacific. It is not a settled proposition to-day; it is taking a long time to build, longer than we expected; and a condition that perhaps could not be foreseen has arisen whereby the Grand Trunk, as I understand it, are not compelled to take over the railroad until the bridge at Quebec has been completed, and to complete that bridge will take some

years. If that is the case, we shall have the National Transcontinental railway on our hands. There is no solution to this situation and it becomes more grievous every day. Therefore', we ought to get ready, by a system of public ownership, to take one road, to couple it up with the Intercolonial, and to deal with the Grand Trunk Pacific if we have to do so. If the Grand Trunk can deal with tihe Grand Trunk Pacific and take it up and give a service with it, so much the better; but, in any event, the country must have one transcontinental line and they must have, in association with that transcontinental controlled by the people, some system of ocean transportation also controlled by the people. We shall soon have the Hudson Bay railway on our hands and we shall have to supply a boat connection for it on the Atlantic. We shall have to get ready for that. There is ho use in building a Hudson Bay railway and then being at the mercy of the steamship lines as we are to-day. There is no use in building canals of 'all kinds in this country, and then being at the mercy of the inland transportation companies, as we are to-day.	In some way we are
in an impasse; but we must find a way out; and if anybody has a suggestion to make which will give the people of this country relief, I would like to know what it is other than public ownership.
We have a problem with the people of the West. The West has come, for a time at least, to somewhat of a standstill, and the people there blame various things for their position. One thing they blame above all things is the exorbitant freight rates. By that they mean ocean freight rates and railway freight rates. This Parliament has actually put them into the condition that they must pay a higher freight rate in the West than, we pay in the East. I have *argued against that for a long time. The railways think they have a right to charge more to the people of the West than to the people of the East. The rapid and quick cure and the way to bring about an equalization of the rates is to have a national road under the control of Parliament and of the people. A national railway can no more discriminate against the people of the West in the matter of transportation charges than we can discriminate against the people of the West in the matter of postage stamps. What is fair for one is fair for the other. Inasmuch as this country has paid for ail these railways and the people of the West have paid their fair share for them, the
people of the West are entitled to equality of rates; and the only way to get equality of rates and improvement in our transportation problem is to nationalize one railway, and to get it into the control of the people. While I do not deprecate the work that the Railway Commission is doing, it is not quite their duty to deal with such a problem as the equalization of rates. That is for Parliament to deal with; and while the railways at present might complain if a reduction in rates were ordered by Parliament, they could not say a word if a reduction in rates were forced by a state-owned railway. Therefore all I have to say at this stage of the debate, although I may (have something more to say later on is, that public ownership of at least one transcontinental Toad is the easiest and the quickest solution of the situation. I take this movement here to-day, small as it may be or great as it may be, as one step in the direction of public ownership as applied to the Canadian Northern railway.

Mr, Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate, I do so with no intention of discussing at any length the resolutions presented to us for our consideration. I do not pretend to be able to handle this great question, involving as it does so many important features of financial intricacies. But, Sir, the discussion that has been going on, the speeches which have already been delivered during this debate, have cleared the air considerably. They have dissipated many misapprehensions which have been expressed throughout Canada during the last few months concerning the financial standing of the Canadian Northern Eailway system, apparently intended to justify in the eyes of the people of this country the action this Government intended to take in this matter. But the speeches in this debate have been of greater value to the people and have given us a great deal of the inside history of the Canadian Northern railway. The hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett), in his eloquent and most interesting speech, told us that a great deal more could be told to this House and the country if only the proper means could be taken to achieve this end. For my part, I should like to have the whole truth and nothing but the truth.
At the outset let me say I absolutely agree with the opinion which has been expressed during this debate that a third transcontinental railway was an ultimate

necessity for this country, if it was not actually a present and immediate necessity. These words to me are words of hope and confidence in the future of this country. It is a policy which has been adopted, it is a hope which I believe is shared by the vast majority of Canadians. But, Sir, this fact alone does not justify us in acting hastily with regard to the resolutions now submitted to us. To-day this Parliament is called upon once more to come to the assistance of the Canadian Northern railway to the extent of $45,000,000. We have been generous to this railway enterprise in the past. We are told that, by this agreement to-day, we are becoming a partner. Then, I say, Sir, it is our first duty as representatives of the people to see what this new partnership means for the people; for we know just what we are going to pay, but we do not know so fully what we are to receive for our money. I go further and say I believe it is our duty, before even discussing the merits of this resolution, to know the men with whom we are called upon to deal. We have been told in this debate that Messrs. Mackenzie and. Mann have given ample evidence of pluck and courage. That is true, and it cannot be denied; and we may say without fear of contradiction that they have shown special zeal in looking after their own interests. For this we cannot blame them-far from it. But their action during the experiences we in this House have had with them should bring us to the view that we also have interests to protect-the interests of the people of Canada. And if we were to go back and review our dealings with these men and the results of those dealings, they could be summarized in one word; that that word would spell 'deception.' Last year we voted millions to the Canadian Northern, but we voted them upon one condition, because we were told that that money would be sufficient to complete the line. To-day these men are again at the door of Parliament seeking new assistance. Last year we were told that if we voted these millions we would have one-tenth of the stock of the Canadian Northern railway. But we have not one-tenth of the stock of the Canadian Northern railway. And' when to-day the Solicitor General comes forward and tells us that by this new arrangement we are to have a two-fifths proprietorship, I ask, what greater guarantee we have this year than we had last year that these terms will eventually materialize? With these fact.? before us, I 
claim that we should pause and we should investigate. Let us know upon what grounds we were deceived last year; we may then be able to prevent a repetition of such actions. Sir, there is no need to hurry this proposal through. Thebe is no financial crisis before us such as has been so vividly portrayed to us by the Tory press of Canada. The Canadian Northern railway can meet their liabilities- Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann tell us so. And these resolutions tell us so, for they stipulate that not a dollar of this $45,000,000 shall go to meet the liabilities of this company. Therefore we can pause and we can investigate, and that is our duty under the present circumstances.
One word about the security we are to receive for this money. In the first place, we are told that we are to have a mortgage on the stock of the subsidiary companies; but we are told that ten of these companies are already mortgaged for $18,000,000. We are told that we are to get a floating mortgage on the property of the Canadian Northern railway. But we see that that property is also mortgaged to the extent of $312,000,000. Then, we are also to have a mortgage on the property of subsidiary companies, but this is limited and will not cover the whole amount of the $45,000,000 we are asked to vote, but every one of these subsidiary companies will have the right to give a mortgage only for that part of the $45,000,000 which is to be expended in the territory in which it operates. And lastly we are to have forty per cent of the common stock of the Canadian Northern railway. As has been said, though we are giving the bulk of the money, we are getting a junior partnership and will have no control. To me this is not satisfactory. The Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen), tells us this is the best security we could have. The hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) tells us that it is a splendid bargain. ,But, immediately after, the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett), rises, and after a four hour speech giving the history of the Canadian Northern railway, he warns us: Do not act hastily, for the basis of these resolutions is deception, and deception again. I say it is our duty to look into these matters; and these contradictions iwe have heard from the other side of the House afford us much stronger reasons for investigating this matter before proceeding any farther.
What has been the result as it has developed from the discussion which we have heard? What will be the position of

Canada? We are told, and it is the only conclusion which we may draw from the arguments which we have heard in this House during this debate, that if we ado.pt these resolutions, if this measure goes through, Canada will be 'fourth mortgage behind an enterprise which is1 already soaked with watered securities and watered stock. For my part I cannot accept these proposals and I intend to vote against them.
There are many other points upon which I would have liked to have touched, which only go to strengthen my conviction that the Government have not safeguarded sufficiently the interests of the people of Canada. If we give assistance that assistance should be coupled with an assurance that the money which we are voting will be used to pay the debts, to complete the line so that these gentlemen will never have to again return to this House for further assistance. I do not believe that that assurance is guaranteed to us in the resolution. Finally, and this is my last grievance, I fail to see why the Government did not exact from the Canadian Northern railway what the Parliament of 1884 exacted from the Canadian Pacific railway under circumstances similar to those of to-day. These promoters-, if they wish to impress faith and confidence in their enterprise upon us sitting here as representatives of the people, should first pledge their personal wealth to the final success of their own work and undertaking.

Mr. Speaker, I shall take but a
few moments to express my views, not so much on the financial character of this transaction as it has been exposed, as on other points. While this discussion is going on in this House the masses of the people of the country are looking upon us as jugglers. They say, and rightly so, that we have been juggling with millions for the last couple of years. Last year we were juggling with $35,000,000, and this year it has been increased by $10,000,000 so that it is now $45,000,000. It is a question whether we are doing right or wrong, but from my .point of view I would strongly favour some of the arguments that have been advanced as to public ownership. If we are to grant the guarantee of $45,000,000 to this- company, or I might say to two men, why not go a little further and establish immediately the public ownership of railways in Canada? There is much to be said against that, and the argument that may be advanced is exactly the same as the argument used so many years ago in European coun-251
tries whenever that question was proposed.
I read only a few days ago that in Switzerland in 1900, 1901 and 1902, when the question of nationalizing the railways was under discussion, much the same arguments were used. In Switzerland as well as in other European countries they bought out the railways from the private companies and for the first year of Government operation in Switzerland there was a large deficit. The existence of this deficit was, of course, used as an argument against Government ownership in other countries where it was proposed. But the movement for the nationalization of railways has been steadily gaining ground in Europe. Railways, have been nationalized in Switzerland, in Germany, in Belgium and in parts of France; and what has been done in those countries can surely be done in this country. Those who use the deficit that occurred in Switzerland on the first year of Government operation as an argument against nationalization always omit to state the cause of that deficit. They omit to state that a large increase of wages was given to the employees of the roads, and also fifty-two days per year of holidays. Of these fifty-two days eight days were consecutive days of holidays without loss of salary. Of course, at the outset, for the first year, there was a deficit. But when we go further in the operation of the road we find that in 1903 there was a surplus larger than the deficit of the first year. I may be told that Switzerland cannot be compared with Canada as it is a small country; but if Government ownership can be conducted in that country with success and if it can be conducted with great advantage in Germany and in Belgium, although Belgium is a small country, I am sure it can be done in this country. If we were to ask the people of Canada today to impose on themselves a tax for the buying of the railways, I am almost sure that a large majority of the electors would respond and state plainly that they were in favour of such an operation. At the present time we are taxing the people indirectly. For instance the guarantee we are liable to pay of this $45,000,000 means $6 on every man, woman and child in the country. If we were to ask an intelligent man, not a member of the House or a man in the same category as Mackenzie and Mann, but a common man of the country, a labourer if you like, if we should impose a mortgage on the head of his little boy, three months old, of $6, what would he say? That is what we are doing by the present method of indirect taxation under



that system. We have a surplus at the end of the year and the Government do not know what to do with it. This year they will have a surplus of $50,000,000 and they feel that they must either diminish the taxation or else spend that money some, how, probably they decided that the best way to dispose of the surplus money that we now have was to grant the guarantee of that $45,000,000.
Mr. A. DeWITT FOSTER:	The hon.
gentleman contends that we are going to pay the $45,000,000 out of the surplus? I do not follow the drift of his argument.

I do not expect that the hon. gentleman will follow my argument. I have stated and I state again that we have a surplus of $50,000,000 in our revenue. That, of course, is in one way a great asset to the country; and so we have the money to guarantee that $45,000,000 which we may become liable to pay. I do not say that we will pay it to-morrow or the next day or next year, but we are liable to have to pay it; and from the arguments I have heard in this House we may as well admit that the Government will be obliged to pay this money.
We have also paid out a large amount of money. It sefems to me that it would have been far better for us to wipe off some of the national debt. We should not be in a hurry over this thing, although the rap at the door of the Government states plainly that they want quick action. I hkve heard it stated during this discussion that many miles of that railroad will have to be rebuilt, and if that is so it will be admitted that it will cost double what it did a few years ago. Some hon. gentlemen have suggested that we should have a commission, but I remember that last year the present Government did not ask for a commission for another line of railway. We have had commission after commission, and I am sure that if a commission had made a report to this House during the present session they would have found a good place for the surplus we now have in the treasury of this country. In passing, ,1 might mention the high cost of living commission, although I know this is not the proper time to discuss that matter. We heard a great deal about the high cost of living commission some months ago, but we have heard nothing about it for a long time now. When the proper time comes we will be able to show just how this commission works. I

have heard, as has every member of this House, that Mackenzie and Mann are worth millions of dollars. There seems to be a very staunch and strong organization among millionaires, which exploits the people of this country through freight rates, and through labour. If there is one reason more than another why I object to Mackenzie and Mann coming to this House, it is because they are members of this get-rich-quick society. They are responsible for the much talked of coal strike on Vancouver Island. It has not been mentioned in this House before, but every member knows that that famous strike was started in the mines of Mackenzie and Mann. If they are so rich, why could they not grant the reasonable demand of the men? Why have they not shown some justice in that matter? That is how they act in the West. Every time Mackenzie and Mann come before this House it seems to me they have more friends than any other company. On two occasions I have heard gentlemen in this House state that they have been indirectly threatened by Mackenzie and Mann. What power is behind their threats? Is it the mighty power of their money, or something else?
I have stated that I am strongly in favour of public ownership. If we do not have public ownership we are indirectly asking the country for direct taxation. I do not know that I would vote to-morrow for direct taxation. If it was proposed to raise $35,000,000 to-morrow for the militia of this country, or say $2 a head, I would probably be against it. Not only are we forcing direct taxation on this country by granting railway and other companies the powers we do grant, but this federal Parliament is becoming a Parliament of private interests. The very rules of this House seem to favour private interests, because if any member of this House wishes to present a matter of public interest the rules debar him from doing so. We are forcing the discontent of the masses of the people in a wrong direction, and sooner or later we must assume the responsibility.
It has been said that we are going into a partnership with Mackenzie and Mann. I, for one, do not want to go into partnership witlh those gentlemen, because if they were absolutely honest I believe they would have put their own fortunes into this enterprise. We are also told that we are going to have forty per cent of the common stock of this company. I have read enough of trusts and mergers and over-capitalization

to know how much that is worth. When a railway is over-capitalized it has to pay dividends on two shares instead of one, and it stands to reason that we must have high freight rates; and it is impossible for the Government, either through the Railway Commission or otherwise, to dictate to these magnates what their freight rates shall be. I would favour even a greater guarantee than this $45,000,000 providing we got control of the company. If it is necessary, let us eliminate altogether Mackenzie and Mann who have been spoken of so often here as ' Sir ' William Mackenzie, and ' Sir ' Donald Mann. I do not believe in that kind of thing, and I am not going to do it; there is too much of it already in this country. If this road can be run by two men, surely it can be run by the Government. Only last year there was a rumour that the Intercolonial railway was to pass into the hands of Mackenzie and Mann. Of course, there would have been a great protest against that as the Intercolonial railway is the only government-owned road in this country. I claim that a government-owned railway should not make any profit. Any one who has read about the government-owned railway system of Australia knows that it has been a great help to the farming industry in that country. The same is true with reference to any other part of Europe where railways are being operated by the Government.
I want to go on record as being against this proposition for the reasons I have just mentioned. I do not want to be charged by the people of this country with having gone into partnership with Mackenzie and Mann. I would rather go into partnership with anybody else than these gentlemen. I would be willing to vote for the expenditure of even a larger amount, if necessary, and I would be willing to appeal to the country on that issue, provided we were starting immediately the government ownership and operation of railways. It was said a moment ago by my hom friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) that we are coming to it. He is right; we are coming to it. I am sure that if there were a referendum on the question of the adoption of public ownership, at least 70 or 75 per cent of the vote cast would be in favour of that proposition. He is right when he states that some years ago he brought this question before the House and that there were then very few to help him. But the people have read since that time, the people have studied, they 'foave become 2514
familiar with the operations of the financial and railway magnates, such as Mackenzie and Mann, which operations have been fully exposed and explained. The light which has been thrown on the subject has driven the great mass of the people to the conclusion that it would be in the interest of the country generally, and particularly in the interest of farming and industrial life, to have public ownership. I simply [DOT]desired to place on record the reason why I am opposed to this grant of $45,000,000 to Mackenzie and Mann and why I am against entering into a partnership with railway magnates of that kind.

DeWITT FOSTER (Kings, N.S.): Mr. Speaker, I do not rise to make any extended remarks upon this subject; but inasmuch as I come from the Maritime provinces, and as the subject under consideration is one of paramount importance to the people of the Maritime provinces, and considering the conditions which have been placed in the resolutions submitted to this House, I feel it incumbent upon me to say a few words in favour of the agreement which the Government has made and to take advantage of the offer that was made by the lion. Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) in his speech the other evening, in which he asked the members of the House, at the proper time, to make any suggestions they might have to better the agreement. It does seem to me that the spirit in which the resolutions were brought before us was the proper spirit for the. introduction of such resolutions to the House and to the country. If there is one feeling apparent on this House on both sides, a feeling that is shared in by every member, it is that this country is face to face with one of the most gigantic problems with reference to the transportation business that we have had to solve or that any government or people has had to solve. There seems to be an accepted realization of this fact on both sides, and there seems to be also a realization of the further fact that something has to be done. That much is admitted by the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), by the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett), and by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle). Bet me say here that these two hon. gentlemen, the hon. member for Calgary -and the hon. member for Kingston, delivered speeches, the equal of which has seldom -been heard, and the superior, rarely within the four walls of this Chamber, if

I can read and judge the speeches that have been placed upon the pages of ' Hansard ' in the past. Volumes of information in detail were given to the House by these hon. members, and while the majority cannot agree with their viewpoint, I, for one, am proud to stand up in my place and say that I 'believe each one of these hon. gentlemen was actuated by the highest possible motives of service to the country, and that, from their own point of view, both performed what they regarded a^ a public duty.
On the opposite side of the House there seems to be a scattering fire directed against these resolutions, but as has been pointed out, that fire is not directed to the principle of the measure which has been brought forward by the Government. From the viewpoint of a young man in politics, it seems a good omen that there are occasions when the sound common sense of both sides of the House, realizing a national duty, will accept the principle of a measure and direct its criticism to working out the details. While the Opposition has a duty to perform in criticising the details of public measures, and while, though our views differ from their's, we must in all fairness submit to such criticisms, it does seem to me that they -are actuated by a desire to perform a service to the country and that all the enthusiasm for public service is not confined to the side which happens to be behind the Government benches.
I have, at the opening of my remarks, to congratulate the Government upon the manner in which they have settled this very serious problem. I am glad to be able to congratulate my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Bo-rden) upon the brave, bold and definite manner in which he has taken up the difficulties that he has found himself confronted with, and has applied himself, together with his colleagues, to the solution of these problems. I have heard nothing so far in the country, nothing from my own constituents, but commendation of the Government for having taken hold of this proposition at a time when the financial conditions were suffering somewhat and at a time when foreign credit could be materially hurt by any failure of the Government to act promptly in dealing with great national problems of which this one, if not the chief. Probably 75,000 or 80,000 men in the old country have put their money into thlfe Canadian Northern proposition, realizing that it was backed by the Government of Canada; whether wisely or

unwisely is a matter of viewpoint. But they put their money into this proposition, and under those -circumstances what would J*e thought of this Government and of this country should that proposition fail and go into the hands of a receiver ? What would be the impression created in the minds of those 70,000 men who had put their money into this enterprise in this young country ? These m-en are l-iving at the very heart of the country to which we will look in the future for a great amount of capital to further develop this country in order that it may take its place amongst the fo-remost nations of the world. What would be the result, I ask ? It does seem to me that nothing short of a panic would be created in the minds of these people and, instead of capital flowing into this country, it would seek an outlet in other directions, where governments, when they embarked upon a proposition, were strong enough to see that proposition was carried out to a successful conclusion. It is a fundamental principle of economics that capital is very shy; men do not put their money into enterprises unless there is a reasonable return and unless that reasonable return is surrounded by safeguards. It is for this reason that those who have money to lend in the old land have invested in Canada, because they have faith in the country and they realized that our railway and municipal securities were safeguarded by the people speaking through their representatives in the Dominion and provincial parliaments. I believe that the Opposition in this House realize that were they in power to-day facing this problem, they would have to do the same as the Government has done. It appears to me that we should set ourselves not so much to carping criticism as towards the task of showing the people of this country the absolute necessity for the proposition which has been presented to the House by the Government, and which has been agreed to in principle by both political parties. I want now, Sir, to address myself for a few moments to a point which I think was admirably taken by the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett), and that is, the question of whether or not this country, with its seven millions of people, is in a position to support three transcontinental railroads with an aggregate of thirty-three thousand miles of rails? I am aware that I shall be confronted at once with the oratory of the right hon. leader of the Opposition, for whose oratory no man in this country has a more profound regard than I. I yield to no man in my admiration for the right hon. leader of the Opposition in certain respects. I am aware that I shall be confronted with his oratory, which will say to me that there are men in this country who believe that if our population is not to be greater than ten millions, these three transcontinental railways are too many. I do not think there is a member in this House, nor is there a thinking man in this country, who believes that Canada will remain with a population of seven millions, or eight millions, or even ten millions.
The normal increase in our population is
400,000	per annum. For a country of this size and of the diversified conditions that we have 400,000 people are far too many foT us to assimilate and to make good citizens of in one year. Supposing we are willing tc grant that Canada will increase at a normal rate as regards population, I take absolutely the same position as the hon. member for Calgary took in saying that this country is not to-day and will not be for some years to come in a position to support three national transcontinental railways with all their branch lines, with all their extensive capitalization, and at the same time to give to the people, what the hon. members from the West on the opposition side of the House have been clamouring for, namely, lower freight rates.

I propose to pat upon 5 Hansard ' a few figures which I have worked out and which are of course subject to correction; but I think they will be admitted by hon. gentlemen as being practically in accordance with the facts. We have to-day in this country about 1,300,000 producers of all classes, of whom, speaking in round numbers, 700,000 are engaged in the business of farming and the balance in manufactures or subsidiary employment, but all are in the class of producers. We have in this country 30,000 miles of railway which, as was pointed out the other night, is the largest mileage in any country on this side of the Atlantic with the same population. That is to say there is one mile of railway for every forty-three producers in this country. I take $102,000 per mile as the capitalization of the Grand Trunk Pacific, $75,000 per mile as the capitalization of the Canadian Pacific and about $60,000 per mile <as the capitalization of the Canadian Northern railway. Taking the average of these three, I get about $75,000 per mile as the average capitalization upon which the railroads must earn their fixed charges upon their bonds and also a dividend to pay the stockholders, whoever they may be, 6 per cent. Some railroads pay more than that, but other roads will pay 6 per cent. Let us take the average dividend on the three systems at 6 per cent, when they get running in good shape, and after paying interest on their bonds. Some one will say that the Canadian Northern railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific will never pay 6 per cent, I am not saying that they will; but 1 say that after they pay the fixed charges of 4 per cent or 4J per cent on their bonds and then pay a dividend on their common stock at the rate of six per cent, we shall have a condition something like this. Forty-three producers in this country will have to support one mile of railway^ the average capitalization of which is $75,000. Suppose that the bonds are at four and one-half per cent and the stock of the company averages one-quarter of the total capitalization, upon which stock six per cent dividend is to be paid. Then, the charges will be at the lowest calculation, $4,500 to $5,000 per mile on each mile of those 30,000 miles of railway. There will be^ therefore, forty-three people taxing themselves for the support of those railroads, and each of them must pay at least $102 per head in order than these railroads may be supported. We have often heard it said in this House during this debate that the security which this Government is getting is of no value.
I shall have only one word to say in regard to that. Whether or not it is of value, I am not competent to judge; but I say that, as far as I can understand from listening to hon. gentlemen on both sides, .it is all the security we can get. I say that though we on this side of the House may have been guilty of that same error of judgment, yet were we not told at the lakt federal election that this Government would be so superior to all others that the people would never hear of such weaknesses, of such sins and crimes as had been imputed to their predecessors? against one of its most cherished pledges, namely that no important legislation would ever be brought in in the dying days of a session.
