Mr. Speaker, I shall not devote any time to answering the speech which has just been made by the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), except to say that the members of His Majesty's loyal Opposition pride themselves on this one thing, that within the ranks of the Liberal party independence of thought is not considered heresy when that thought differs from the opinion of the *majority of the party to which we belong. I ain sure I am speaking for every member of the Opposition when I say that no gentleman on this side of the House will be put up or will stand up during the course of this debate and try to read out of the ranks of the Liberal party, because of his difference from us on this question, our very much esteemed friend from Norfolk.
Listening to this discussion for the last few days, there are certain grounds of common agreement between the members of this House, I presume, on both sides. One could not but be struck by the unanimity of opinion on one important feature

of this question, namely, Canada's duty at the moment in reference to this national undertaking. In so far as my position is concerned, I want to say that any criticism or unfavourable expression of opinion I may offer in reference to the resolution that the House is considering is not attributable to any failure to appreciate the duty of Canada to come to the aid of this great undertaking if this undertaking requires that aid and if we propose to give it in the proper way. I am sure that we all recognize the necessity of a third transcontinental railway. The time has passed for the .members of this House to give that question any extended consideration. Canada is already committed, by the Acts of previous Parliaments, to the building of a third transcontinental railway, namely, the Canadian Northern. I must disagree with some expressions of opinion by certain hon. gentlemen opposite as to this proposition and as to the necessity for a third system.
I cannot conceive that the Canadian Northern Railway system could ever have been a great system as compared with the Canadian Pacific or the Grand Trunk Pacific if its operations had been bottled up in the three western prairie provinces. There is this to be said for the eastern line of this railway, that it travels through a country that, in my judgment, no member of this House has demonstrated will be devoid of traffic producing results. I noticed in the newspapers recently a statement to the effect that on the Transcontinental railway west of Quebec and east of Cochrane already a great colonizing move-' ment has developed. By the political opponents of the National Transcontinental railway we were led to believe that that line would pass through a great wilderness that would never amount to anything in the way of producing traffic. Within the past two months that idea has been dispelled and I would look upon the eastern section of the Canadian Northern which travels through the great clay belt of northern Ontario as being a part of the railway that in time will be a profit producing undertaking.
In my judgment this question ought to be considered by this House as a straight business proposition. Personally, it -would be absolutely impossible for me to express an unfriendly sentiment against the Canadian Northern Railway system, because I come from a part of the country that owes its being almost to the development of the Canadian Northern Railway system, its main line and

branches. The history of the Canadian Northern railway in western Canada is a history that spells very largely the history of the development of northern Manitoba, northern Alberta and northern Saskatchewan, and while it is true that in the northern parts of my own province we have to-day the Grand Trunk Pacific and certain lines of the Canadian Pacific railway, it is a well-known fact that the enterprise of Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann and the development of that enterprise in the building of the Canadian Northern and its tributary branches, is responsible for the branch line policy Of the Canadian Pacific railway itself. Everybody knows that for years the Canadian Pacific railway in western Canada played a dog in the manger policy and attempted to make the people coming into western Canada subject to the main line of that railroad, and refused to send branches out into the northern part of these three prairie provinces. But in 1903, with the advent of the extension of the Canadian Northern system westward, we found that the Canadian Pacific railway wakened up. They came to the conclusion that if this new railroad system was going to open up that country they had better get busy and send a few feeders in that direction too. So that, as a result of the development of the Canadian Northern Railway system in the prairie provinces, we have had the development of the other great transcontinental systems. In any criticism of the proposals that are before us at the present time, in view of the history of western Canada and of its development, and especially the developments of the northern part of the three prairie provinces, I am bound to say that for my part I can only have admiration far the enterprise of the men who when others refused to build railroads into that section of the country came forward-it is true with Government help-to supply it with railroads. They had the vision to see the possibilities of these districts that were not served by railroads, and, by Government aid if you will, they extended lines through that great productive area.
When the Canadian Northern main line was extended westward to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, the people began to come into these provinces in large numbers. They did not stay along the main line but they spread out in various districts throughout the north. It then became immediately necessary far somebody to build branch lines, feeders to the main line of the Canadian Northern, and after
the formation of the province of Saskatchewan and Alberta the Governments of these two provinces found themselves confronted with this very serious condition; that we had the main line of the Canadian Northern running through the northern portions of these provinces, and away beyond that main line, forty miles, fifty miles, sixty miles, even a hundred miles, there were settled numbers of people who required service from branch lines. In 1908 the representatives of the Saskatchewan Government came to the Government of Canada and asked for assistance towards the building of a number of branch lines ini that province. The Government of the day said to the representatives of the .Saskatchewan Government: you have set up housekeeping for yourselves; up to the present time the federal Government has given aid to the main line and to some branches, but we have gone far enough in giving aid to these branch lines in these new provinces which now have their own governments by virtue of their organization into provinces. The provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were confronted with the problem that they had to do something in order to serve the needs of the people by the building of branch lines that would be feeders to the main line of the Canadian Northern railway. The result was that for three or four years, from 1908 to 1912, the province of Saskatchewan undertook to meet the needs of the people by guaranteeing the bonds of branch lines that were authorized by Acts of this Parliament. That is to say, they guaranteed the bonds of lines that were to be constructed under Dominion charters. But in 1912 the Saskatchewan Government went a step further and they incorporated the Canadian Northern Saskatchewan Railroad Company, and in the session of 1912 the legislature of Saskatchewan not only authorized the building of several hundred miles of branch lines in the province, under this Act, hut they actually guaranteed the bonds of 255 miles of these branch lines. It has been pointed out in this House already that under that company's charter up to the present time, from 1912 to 1914, the Canadian Northern have actually only commenced construction on thirty miles out of a total of 255, miles, the bonds of which were guaranteed in the session of 1912. Therefore, for t'he last two years there has been very little development on the part of the Canadian Northern railway in the prairie provinces; I speak particularly for the province of Saskatchewan. What I want

to point out to the people of my own province who are anxious to see the branch lines of the Canadian Northern system in that province extended to the various districts that require these facilities, is that one very serious fault that I find with the proposals now before the House is that in my judgment there is absolutely no provision made for the extension of these branch lines. Further than that, in the consideration of these resolutions, I find that not only is there no provision for the building of these branch lines, so much required by the people of the West, but that by this proposal the Dominion Government purports to take away from the people of Saskatchewan and from the people of my province the rights which they took unto themselves by the incorporation of the Canadian Northern Saskatchewan Railway Company, and by the guaranteeing of 255 miles of their branch lines. If I read these resolutions aright this Canadian Northern Saskatchewan Company is declared to be, with a number of other constituent companies, a work for the general advantage of Canada, and here is the position that that places my province in.
We have, as I said, in one session of our legislature, guaranteed bonds for 255 miles to the extent of $15,000 a mile. By our agreement with the Canadian Northern railway, the Government of the province of Saskatchewan is given the right of decision as to the location of those lines and of the stations, the right of decision as to the standard of the road and the standard of equipment; and also, by virtue of the Saskatchewan Railway Act, the Government have the control of their own rates. Now we have this legislation proposed by the Prime Minister, in which he declares that the Canadian Northern Saskatchewan Railway Company is to be hereafter a work for the genera] advantage of Canada. When we have about thirty miles out of that 255 miles constructed, this Government comes along and says, ipso fac-to: All these 255 miles of proposed lines will hereafter be adjudged works for the general advantage of Canada. What does that mean, so far as the people of my province are concerned? It means that, with regard to every mile of the unfinished, the untouched part of the Canadian Northern Saskatchewan system, instead of the provincial Government having the right to decide as to location of lines and stations, and so on, this Government have that right of decision. In other words, the

Government of the province of Saskatchewan guarantee the bonds, pay the piper, take the responsibility of guaranteeing $15,000 a mile for every mile of that railroad, and yet the Minister of Railways o' the Dominion of Canada shall determine where those roads are to be built. In my judgment, this constitutes an absolute and flagrant breach of provincial rights, and should not be tolerated by this Parliament, especially by members of this Government, who have always, as I have understood it, posed before the people of this country as the champions of provincial rights throughout the length and breadth of Canada.
Where is this going to stop is the question that we in the western provinces are asking. In the province of Saskatchewan we have incorporated a company, authorized hundreds of miles of lines to be constructed and guaranteed some hundreds of miles. That company will be no longer under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Railways of the Government of Saskatchewan. We may, at the next session of the Saskatchewan Legislature organize a new company and give it authority to build some more hundreds of miles. We may guarantee the bonds of that line. Yet, according to the precedent that this Government is establishing in this legislation, no sooner has that company been organized and its bonds guaranteed, than this Government and this Parliament can declare that, the works of that company are works for the general advantage of Canada, and so the province of Saskatchewan will again find itself face to face with the situation where it must pay the piper, where it must guarantee the notes of the railway company that wants to build a line in our province, and yet receive absolutely no quid pro quo for the expenditure that it so makes. In my judgment, it is one of the very serious objections that we in the West must find against this arrangement as proposed in the resolutions now before the House.
I have said that this legislation, m my judgment, offers no encouragement to the people of the prairie provinces who want to see money expended in the building and betterment of branch lines in our provinces. Not a dollar, so far as I can figure out from the terms of the resolution, is to be devoted to that purpose. We know perfectly well who will have to pay. We are going to put $45,000,000 more into the Canadian Northern railway towards com-

The charge has very often been laid at the door of our provincial governments in the West that they are too extravagant in the building of branch lines; that they are guaranteeing too many bonds and going too deeply into this policy. When we are faced by this situation that the Dominion Government promotes the building of great main lines of railways throughout our provinces; when, as a result of that policy, the people come from all quarters of the globe to settle up our prairies; when they get here and settle miles and miles away from our main lines of railway, will any one tell me what the governments of those provinces can do except to continue the policy that they have already inaugurated, namely, the guaranteeing of bonds for branch lines in those provinces? So far as the province from which I come is concerned, while it is true that we have guaranteed the bonds of several hundred miles of branch lin'es in that province, our policy has fallen far short of the necessities of the situation, if these people are to have reasonable transportation facilities in that part of the country.
I know there is a sentiment in the prairie provinces in favour of the Government of Canada doing something to assist the Canadian Northern railway. He says that there is no such company, that all the companies known at the present time are included in schedule 1; but it is not violent supposition that there may be other companies which have charters for roads more or less connected with the Canadian Northern, and which may perhaps be brought later on into the Canadian Northern system, or which certain promoters may be thinking of bringing in. You are giv'.rg to the Governor in Council the power to bring any such company into the system, and Parliament has no power to exercise any control over the will of the Governor in Council. The Governor in Council is supreme in this; and, whether its action is wise or unwise, there is no method by which you can prevent it or criticise it after it has taken place. I can conceive-and it is not a violent supposition-that there may be, even at this very moment, companies which have perhaps not made application to my right hon. friend at present, but which are awaiting only the passing of this Bill to come in and endeavour to be taken into this system. I submit for the consideration of my right hon. friend that such a power is not consistent with the object which he 
has in view at the- present time, which is to establish the Canadian Northern Railway system. The Canadian Northern Railway system, as it exists at present, is well-known. We know the companies which ought to be taken into that system; and, if at the present time they have all been taken in, it is all right; but if it is contemplated that some other companies, the existence of which we do not suspect, may be brought in, I do not see why you should take such an extraordinary precaution as to give this power to the Governor in Council, when the hon. gentleman who has charge of the Bill says: I know nothing of any companies that may be brought in. The legislation which we are considering to- [DOT] day is for a special object, namely, as stated in the preamble of the resolution, to unite under one management all the companies which are now under the control of the firm of Mackenzie and Mann. It ought not to be extended beyond that; and I cannot see, unless better reasons are given than have been given by my hon. friend the Solicitor General, why such an extraordinary provision as that should be included and why such powers should be vested in the Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I see nothing of the extraordinary character which my hon. friend finds in the proposal. As far as I understand it, it seems to be this: There may and doubtless in the future will be railways incorporated under charters, perhaps to be created in the future, which, although practically and in effect and physically forming part of the Canadian Northern Railway system, will nevertheless be not legally part of that system. The idea was to make provision that those railways, when they came into existence, might be legally made part of the Canadian Northern system. That does not seem to be a very extraordinary or unusual power. As my right hon. friend, however, finds some difficulty about it, we will let that clause stand for the moment and go o.n>
to the next.

Under this agreement
the Canadian Northern is to be given running rights over the Intercolonial railway. There are many branch lines or lines that touch the Intercolonial. Under this clause could the Canadian! Northern lease the best of those lines, attach them to the Canadian Northern in connection with the running rights over the Intercolonial, and have that ratified?
Not under this clause.
Under any clause?
They could not do anything whatever of that nature without the consent of the Governor in Council.
Is the Governor in Council taking the right to do what I have explained may be done? If so, you aire asking for too much power.

This is just a beginning of the Government becoming a partner in a private-owned concern; and I will tell the right hon. the leader of the Government . that this is only a beginning and a very small beginning; that he cannot be or the Government of Canada cannot be a partner in a private-owned transcontinental railway. (Reading):
' Constituent companies ' means such of those companies mentioned in the first schedule to the following resolutions, and such other companies, hereafter declared by the Governor in Council to be comprised in the Canadian Northern system, as own or operate railways, terminals, bridges or other railway faci'.ites.
That means every company which the promoters of the Canadian Northern railway, who are the controllers of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, may bring into that concern. If they do not make default, the Government is absolutely in the hands of Mackenzie and Mann who own and control stock hereafter in large and small enterprises in which they have an interest, or which they may undertake to exploit throughout this country.

In regard to subsidiary companies, I would like to ask my hon. friend the Solicitor General, for my own information, why he has made a difference between constituent companies and subsidiary companies? Subsidiary companies are those which do not operate railways, and constituent companies are those which do operate railways. So far as the object of the legislation is
11 p.m. concerned, I have not been able to 'see why this difference is preserved. There may be a difference between constituent companies and subsidiary companies legally or in any other way, which I have not been able to find out on reading over the resolution; but it seems to me simply to make the resolution more cumbersome than is necessary. I think we should call them all constituent companies or all subsidiary companies. I understand
very well the distinction, but I do not see the object of it.
There is one section in which the distinction is essential. I will find it and show it to the right hon. gentleman.

In regard to contractors, I want to ask the Prime Minister if there will be any objection to amending that portion of the interpretation clause so that it will include Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann. In discussing the general resolution, I pointed out yesterday that section 4 of the resolution simply said:
That covenants or undertakings to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council shall he given that all outstanding temporary lor ns to the Canadian Northern or any of its constituent or subsidiary com; anies secured... will be paid-
I pointed out that there were a large number of securities which were doubtless collateral; but that, in my opinion, and I think I proved it pretty well-those collaterals would not pay the debts. I suggested that section 4 be amended by inserting the words, ' by the contractors ' after the word ' undertakings ', so that the section would read as follows:
That covenants or undertakings by the contractors to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council-
Then you would have Mackenzie and Mann personally responsible that these debts would be paid. Again in section 5
the same matter comes up:

That covenants or undertakings of the contractors and such other covenants or undertakings as may be required by the Governor in Council shall be given that the current indebtedness of the Canadian Northern and of the said constituent and subsidiary companies will within one year from the passing of the Act to be based upon these resolutions he reduced to the normal or usual current amount- which I think has been estimated here at about $3,000,000. If the word ' contractors ' included Mackenzie and Mann personally, you would have the personal covenant of Mackenzie and Mann that these debts would be paid. If these constituent companies and subsidiary companies are all allowed to stand as they are now, then we are giving Mackenzie and Mann the right to bring into this system anything whatever, no matter whether it be a railway company, bridge company, a coal mine or anything else. If we bring this in, we saddle these upon the country, for once they are in the sys-

tem, the country has got to pay the liability. You can bring in almost anything in Canada, so long as it is a corporation, into this system, and the country becomes responsible to finance that scheme-we have to pay the bills. Yet Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann personally are not responsible for a dollar. It does seem to me that the Prime Minister should consider this very carefully and if necessary allow it to stand. I think it a very important matter, because if what I suggest were done it would take away a great deal of the objection that members on this side, and people all over the country, have to this measure.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As I understand it, under section 4, and under section 5, as well, it is competent for the Governor in Council to require the personal undertaking of Sir William Mackenzie or Sir Donald Mann, or both.
But would it not be better if we had the assurance in the legislation that it would be required?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not see that it is necessary.

I would ask why it is that the parties of the fourth part in the agreement, called the ' contractors ' include Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann, while in the interpretation clause the word ' contractors ' means Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited.
That is# easy to be answered-it is because in the agreement Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann are only covenanting to hand over stock and not to put in a claim for their services.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend is mistaken.	' .	:	j

Well, it might go a little farther. I stated it yesterday. In the first place they agree to transfer $33,000,000 of stock to the Government; then to transfer the Brockville and Westport line free of charge, and to sign whatever other agreement is necessary to carry out the agreement; and also not to put in a claim for their services. That is all. When they include these gentlemen personally and make them responsible, it is only to hand over stock and carry out these other things that I have stated. When their covenant is to pay money, they are personally carefully left out of the term ' contractors.' I

think the hon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), is very well justified in calling the attention of the committee to the condition of affairs.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is for the reason I have already explained. It is hardly correct to say that they are left out, because the provisions of sections 4 and 5 are absolutely sufficient to have them included. So far as the agreement is concerned in which Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann are personally and individually made parties, the mere proviso of the clause of the agreement will indicate reasons why they should be parties in that way. Subsection (e) of section 2 provides for the absolute release of all contractors' profits, commissions and claims of every kind against the Canadian Northern railway or against any of the constituent or subsidiary companies. It was for the reason that it was desired to include not only Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, but also Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann individually in respect of these claims that they were made parties as well as the corporation itself, and therefore the clause in the agree-. ment has that operation.

Have records been brought down containing information as to who are the shareholders and officers of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited? If not, I think that information should be laid before the committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I could not say at the moment whether the information laid before the committee comprises that or not. But I should think there would be no difficulty about getting it.

I submit to the right hon. gentleman that this section should stand until we have that information. I think that is only reasonable. We cannot give a legislative definition of the meaning of the word 'contractors,' declaring it to be a certain company without knowing who are the persons in that company.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The persons in the corporation may transfer their stock to-morrow, or may have transferred it yesterday.
But that information would be interesting-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Interesting, perhaps, but it does not alter the legal position in the slightest, because the transfer of shares does not affect the entity of the corporation.

The Prime Minister has stated with practical accuracy the effect of subsection e of section 2 of the agreement. No doubt Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann personally release all these companies from any claim for their services. But it is also true that they do not become responsible for the payment of any money. The right hon. gentleman says the Government might demand it under the covenants and undertakings in sections 4 and 5. Eut why will not the Prime Minister say that he will demand it? Why will not he say that when the covenants are drawn up Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann will be made personally responsible? And, if he gives that agreement, why will he not go so far as to put it in the document itself? If this were done the country would have it in the legislation, and the very word 'contractors' would mean that they were personally responsible.

Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, is a limited liability company. But Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann individually may have enormous wealth without having any personal liability in respect of this corporate institution. In my opinion the suggestion made by the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., (Mr. Carvell) is one which should receive not only the attention of the committee but the approval of the Government, and Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Marnn individually should be made liable, and not merely as a limited liability company. It might be that you *could not get a dollar from them as a limited liability company, but each of them is known to be a millionaire many times over and capable not only of financing this institution and building this road but of building another transcontinental road as well.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen laugh,
but public opinion is-and we all know it- that Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann are able to build a railway if they want to do it. There is no necessity of smiling over it or making it an object of mirth. We know that each of them is a multi-millionaire, and they have made money out of the railway manipulation. I make that statement here as a member of this House and no man. dare challenge it.
I challenge, it absolutely; the hon. gentleman is making .a statement without foundation in fact. The evidence before the House is contrary to what the hon. gentleman says.

The hon. member for
Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol) is quite in error in his notion. Both Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann are men of great wealth, which they have made out of the manipulation of Canadian Northern railway transactions. Now, it is asked that they should be made personally liable in regard to these matters. They are being made liable as a limited liability company. And the hon. member for Carleton suggests that they should be made liable individually.
I believe that the Government .should include under the term ' contractors ' not only Mackenzie, Mann and 'Company, Limited, but also 'Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann.

I wish to add my request to those already preferred from this side of the House. I think the Prime Minister will concede that we should not proceed so fast with this particular clause that we have been discussing till, in the first place, the information asked for by the hon. member for Pictou is brought down, that is that we should have full particulars regarding the composition of the firm of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, the names of those who compose it, the capital stock of the company, and generally all such information as would enable us to determine just what value is to be placed upon any guarantee that may _ be given by that particular company. In addition to 'that, I think the request made by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) is a very reasonable one, that is, that within this definition of the word ' contractors ' should be placed Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann, individually. In fact, in view of the discussion that has taken place in the past week, and more particularly in view of the disclosures made by the Government supporters from Calgary and Kingston, I do not think it would be going too far, in fact I think we would only be discharging our first duty, if we asked that in the definition of the word ' contractors ' there should also be included the Northern Construction Company. As I understand it, that company is practically Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann. The company has done an enormous amount of work, if my



information be correct, and I submit it is the business of Parliament, now that these resolutions have reached the committee, to throw around this agreement all the safeguards that we can possibly avail ourselves of. I do not think, even if the information asked for by the hon. member for Pictou and that asked by the hon. member for Carleton be granted, we will be going too far in asking that ithe definition of this word should include the Northern Construction Company also.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman is mistaken about the Northern Construction Company, because I am informed that neither Sir William Mackenzie nor Sir Donald Mann has the slightest interest in that company, directly or indirectly; in fact, if I remember correctly, I read a declaration from the persons who are the officers of that company-
That they had not received any profits from it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That they had no interest in it whatever, either direct or indirect. That is my recollection.

I have a great deal of faith in the proposition I am placing before the House. I think it is a very material contention. It has been stated here a great many times by my friends opposite that the Canadian Northern system has reached the point where it is compelled to get assistance from some person, and the only person from whom it can obtain assistance is the Government of Canada. That seems to be admitted by all hon. gentlemen opposite, and I think there is no question about it. They have, as has been stated, received nearly $244,000,000 of money from somebody, and they say it has all gone into the system. They say it will take about another $100,000,000 to complete the system, and that they have $58,000,000 of good assets available once we furnish the $58,000,000 to make it liquid, and then all the rest of their assets will become saleable and the country will never lose a dollar; everything will be taken care of, and our $40,000,000 will become one of the greatest assets of Canada. If our friends have such faith as this, and if Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann have such faith, it cannot do any harm to include them in the definition of the word ' contractors ' and make them personally responsible, not for the completion of the road but for the loans now secured and also the loans from the
fMr. Murphy. ]
banks. I would like to have these gentlemen become personally responsible that these loans will be taken care of. In order to place the matter before the committee in concrete form, I would move:
That the definition of contractors be amended by adding thereto the words 'Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald D. Mann.'

I have taken the ground in the few words I have said on this matter, that Mackenzie and Mann, to the extent of their financial ability, be it more or less, should go in behind this undertaking with their own personal means. It is their undertaking; we have put up most of the money but still the majority of it remains their undertaking. I think we are not asking too much in insisting that they, as practical owners of this concern, put in their personal obligation with ours; and believing that to be only fair to the people of Canada, I am prepared to vote for this amendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: When the hon. gentleman suggests that Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann have not pledged their personal credit in connection with this enterprise, he is absolutely misinformed. Anything that might be called the working capital in connection with the construction of this road, and this amounts to a great many million dollars, has been raised, as I understand, not only by Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, but, in many cases, upon the individual credit of Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann.
Not a dollar on their individual credit.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I can only say that my information does not correspond with that of my hon. friend.
Will the Prime Minister be good enough to point out in the records placed before us where either gentleman is responsible for a dollar?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Will the hon. member
point out anything in the record that is against that? I was dealing with a statement made by the hon. member for South Renfrew who has stated, and a great many hon. gentlemen in this House have asserted the same thing, that the position of Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann differed from the position of those who came to Parliament in 1884, in that these men had pledged their individual credit in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway enterprise, while Sir William Mackenzie

and Sir Donald Mann have not done so. I say I am perfectly satisfied that that statement is not accurate, and that the working capital for the construction of this road, running into many millions of dollars, has been provided in the way suggested, and we know that ten and a half million dollars, representing half the contractors' claims outstanding, has been raised and provided for. Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, in connection with this agreement, propose to give security to the satisfaction of the Government in respect of what are called the temporary loans and the floating indebtedness. We realize that Mackenzie and Mann must pledge their own assets to a certain extent; indeed, to a very large extent and we have provided by this agreement that they shall do that. In addition to that, we have insisted that Mackenzie and Mann shall risk everything in this enterprise in this respect: that every dollar which otherwise they might have been able to claim against this company in the way of commission or agency work, covering a period of a great many years, shall be absolutely released, and I have no doubt whatever, as I have said in this House before, that that claim would have run into many millions of dollars. So, under the circumstances, I do not think it is a fair case to say that their individual and personal credit has not been pledged. I maintain that it has been pledged, and that the construction of this road could not have been carried on unless it had been pledged to a very large extent indeed.

This is a very important feature of the case. On the one hand we have the statement of the right hon. Prime Minister that Mackenzie and Mann have pledged their credit individually, and on the other hand the statements of members on both sides of the House that they have not pledged'their credit, individually. Is this not a case calling for some little investigation? If it be true, as has been said, that Mackenzie and Mann individually are deeply interested in enterprises in Mexico, Brazil, in townsites in Montreal, and in traction companies in the cities of Winnipeg, Toronto, and Vancouver, I say that they should put up something as security themselves. Personally, I do not know whether these are facts, but the statement has been made over and over again by the hon. member for Calgary, the hon. member for Kingston, and other members. Why should we not have an investigation to find
out if they really are the possessors of such large incomes? For my part, if I knew that Mackenzie and Mann had practically nothing outside of their interests in the Canadian Northern railway I would certainly alter my mind in regard to these resolutions, ibut I am morally convinced that one of these gentlemen at least is a multi-millionaire, as was stated by the hon. member for Calgary. In these hard times when money is so scarce, and there is so much unemployed, I say it is not becoming on the part of the Government to take all the chances and all the responsibilities, and to allow these multi-millionaires to reap all the benefits.

It is really inspiring to hear the hon. member for Kouville, now that he is a private member, dilate on multi-millionaires and the necessity of getting their covenants in railway undertakings. It has been the policy of Canada ever since there was a Canada to consider railway undertakings as public utilities in which the people as a people are interested, as well as merely business undertakings in which those engaged in them are interested. As a consequence of that, the policy of this country has been to assist railway undertakings. The Canadian Pacific has been assisted by subsidies, and the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Northern railway have been assisted by subsidies and by guarantees. When was it first promulgated by the Liberal party or by the hon. member for Eouville that these railway companies should not be assisted by subsidies or by guarantees unless they were owned by men who had absolutely no other possessions whatever outside the railway company? That doctrine has never been pronounced until to-night. Before a railway company got assistance from the late Government I presume an inquiry was held to see that the stockholders of that company did not possess a dollar beyond their stock in the company. Was that the policy of the late Government? If not, his argument cannot possibly stand.

It is not a parallel
case.
There is nothing parallel now.	.
Why do you not discuss the agreement.

I know my hon. friend likes to get away from his votes when he was on the Government side of the House. The question before the committee is this-

what is fair and reasonable under the circumstances? And in discussing what is fair and reasonable and the bona fides of hon. gentlemen opposite, it is not out of the way to remind them that three years ago Mackenzie and Mann, as owners of the Canadian Northern Ontario railway, were before this House and got the approval of hon. gentlemen opposite, and of the hon. member for Eouville as a member of the Government, to a bond guarantee of $35,000,000 and that Government never inquired whether Mackenzie and Mann had put their own money into the road. If they were wealthy men at that time-and I presume	they	had	investments inMexico	and	South	America	then
-why did the Government of that day not insist that they put up those investments before they called on the Government of this country for a guarantee? Why did gentlemen opposite not take a chase around the universe to see if Mackenzie and Mann owned a horse in one continent and stock in another, before they came to their assistance in 1911?
Does not my hon. friend see a difference? In 1911, the country got a first mortgage as security, and in 1914 it is getting practically no security.

Why, then, did the
country have to pledge its credit at all in 1911. If the company was solid in 1911, why could they not go to the money markets for their money? If the doctrine is good now it was good then. Mackenzie and Mann got a bond guarantee from the late Government in 1911, and the bon. member for South Renfrew did not inquire what they had outside the railway.
They gave us a first mortgage, which you have not got.

The hon. member for
South Renfrew takes this position, that any one who offers the Parliament of Canada a first mortgage will get the aid he requires.
Not at all.

The question is, what
is fair and proper between the public and the promoters? What have we done in this case? We have heard a great deal of the private property pledged by the owners of the Canadian Pacific railway. I hold no brief for Mackenzie and Mann nor for the Canadian Northern railway. We are the trustees of the people of Canada and the conduct of these gentlemen 
only comes in question so far as it relates to the merits of this Bill and of the Government's proposal. I say I believe it will be found that what Mackenzie and Mann have pledged of their own assets, not derived from the Canadian Northern railway in any way, towards the success of the Canadian Northern railway transcends, and far transcends, what was pledged by the promoters of the Canadian Pacific railway.
What have they pledged?

The hon. member is
very anxious to know what they have pledged. They have pledged 4,102,009 acres of land.
Which never belonged to them.

What was it given to
them for?

The hon. member for
Welland says it never belonged to Mackenzie and Mann, and the hon. member for Carle-ton asks me why the land was given. I cannot answer both at once.
Answer one at a time.

Mackenzie and Mann took over the charters of three railway companies, and upon completing the works called for by those charters were entitled, by the law that gave the charters, to the land grants. They completed the work and became the owners of the land grants for completing the work, they turned over these land grants to the Canadian Northern and when -the Canadian Northern Railway Company was formed as a company the lands were granted to the Canadian Northern Railway Cbmp-an-y. But the grants that went with the -charters went with the completion of the railways, they completed the railways -and therefore were entitled to the lands. Does my hon. friend say that there was no legal title to these lands, that they did not earn them?
I would like to ask my hon. friend a -question.

I am -asking my hon-..
friend to answer mine.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask hi-m a question?
Not now; answer min<e-first.

I say they axe not entitled to the land. Now, will my hon. friend allow me to ask him ai question?
Mr. ME1GHEN:	Now, we will follow
that up.

I have answered my
hon. friend's question; will he allow me to ask him a question?

I will allow the hon.
gentleman to ask me a question when I come to it and I will not do what he did yesterday-promise to come to it and never get there. My hon. friend says	that	they	were not
entitled to it, that they never were in a position to make title to those 4,102,000 acres of land. Let me ask him how is it that they have made title to these 100,000 acres of land of which they own part to-day and have sold part, the titles to which have never been questioned.
Go on.

Now, I am ready for
my hon. friend's question.

I am very much obliged to my hon. friend the 'Solicitor General, I. am sure. The question I want to ask him is if there were not securities upon these roads when they got them .and if the Government or the Canadian Northern Railway Company is not responsible to-day to pay these securities.
On the roads?

Certainly, on the roads. My hon. friend says that Mackenzie and Mann bought certain roads in Manitoba that carried a land grant. They got the land grant and they were not bound to give it over to the system. We have their mortgages and bonds on these roads, they are there to-day, they have to be paid and I would ask my hon. friend, is not the Canadian Northern system liable to pay them?
I did not say that they bought the roads, but I did say that they bought the charters to build the roads and that when they built the roads they became entitled to the land grant.

We have to pay the
securities.
They built the roads out of the money derived from the sale of the land.

How is it then that
the Canadian Northern got the land?

Are the mortgages on
the roads then?
Certainly, these parts became parts of the Canadian Northern and are subject to all the mortgages on the Canadian Northern.
Why should not the land go to pay the mortgages?

Because the men who built the road were entitled to the land for building them. They built them and earned the land in the same way as the hon. gentleman would earn his fee in a legal case. If they did not earn them they could not give titles to them. They did give titles to them to the Prairie Land Company to whom they had transferred about 50,000 acres. Consequently, they were the owners of the 4,102,000 acres and they turned them in. I will give my hon. friend a very similar instance that will bring the matter abruptly to his mind. The Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway Company also had a land grant which they got to construct the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan. The promoters of the road were entitled to the land grant for the construction of the road. They constructed the road and earned the land grant. An hon. member on the other side of the House was one of those promoters and they became interested in that land grant, transferring the road and did not transfer the land grant.
And another hon. gentleman on the other side of the House.

And another hon. gentleman on this side. They were doing what they were perfectly entitled to do, because they were the owners of the land grant as they were itihe owners of the road, subject to whatever was against the road. Does the hon. gentleman say that his colleague on that side of the House did something dishonourable when he disposed of his own property in the shape of the land which he had earned? Then why does he say that these gentlemen are doing something which they are not justified in doing?
I did not expect my hon. friend the Solicitor General to get into such a heat as he has over this matter.
Oh, oh.

I thought we were putting up a very fair business proposition.

and it is such a good business proposition that my hon. friend cannot answer it without getting ugly over it.
I did not get ugly.
Your manner belied you, then.
I might have looked it.

Yes, you looked it.
There is no parallel between this case and that of the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway Company. Twenty years ago that road was sold but the land did not go with the road. Mackenzie and Mann saw fit to buy that road seven or eight years ago, and they bought it without the land. If they had got the land with it they would have had a more valuable asset.
That is not the question. How did the men who got the land manage to get it?

I will come to that. Seven or eight years ago the Canadian Northern, or Mackenzie and Mann, bought that road. They did not buy the land with it, hut they bought the road with a mortgage against it, and we are going to pay the mortgage. It is a pity we did not get the right to the land with it. But Mackenzie and Mann never owned this land, and were never in a position to sell it or to hand it over to the Government. If Mackenzie and Mann had any land with reference to other roads it was because they built the roads and got the land grants. They mortgaged the roads, and the mortgages are on these roads to-day. They are handing over to the Government these mortgages so that the Government will be responsible for the payment of them. I did not think my hon. friend would commence hair splitting so early in the game. My hon. friend tries to draw a distinction between holding a title and the word ' entitle.' He asked me if they were entitled to this land and I said ' no,' and then he asked me, in order to make a legal quibble, how they got this hundred thousand acres of land if they had not a title to it. I want to give my hon. friend a little advice-
Oh, oh.

My hon. friend will get these resolutions through a great deal easier by meeting us in a bigger and broader manner than by trying to draw these hairsplitting distinctions between a legal title and the question whether they are entitled to these lands. Let us try and get back now to the point at issue and talk business:
Exercise a little common courtesy yourself.

I think my hon. friend had better get out and look after his Hindus that are landing in Vancouver. He has got all that he can attend to, and he has got his work cut out looking after the Hindus who are landing. If I want any advice from him, I will ask him for it.
Our Hindus are equal to the hon. gentleman.

I am sorry I cannot return the compliment. Now, we will leave him out of the question. I would like to come back to the amendment we have moved, because after all that is the important thing? Why do the Solicitor General and the leader of the House object to Mackenzie and Mann personally becoming responsible to pay these debts?
I was getting to it.

The Solicitor General
could not get to the South Pole by travelling north. There must be some reason why they object to Mackenzie and Mann giving personal guarantees. I want the Solicitor General to point out where in these resolutions is there any statement that Mackenzie and Mann will become personally responsible for anything. There is not a word anywhere to that effect. The only inference is that Mackenzie and Mann would not become personally responsible, and the Government did not intend to ask them to do so. If the Government is sincere, and if Mackenzie and Mann are sincere, they ought not to be afraid to become responsible for the payment of the debts. If these securities, which are now pledged as collateral for these debts will not pay them, then as a matter of justice Mackenzie and Mann ought to be compelled to pay them, and if they have not sufficient property to pay off this debt, it is their misfortune and the country will have to become responsible. That is the whole issue.

I was in the middle of a speech which it will not be necessary for me to finish now; I was setting out to show that Mackenzie and Mann had contributed a great deal to this enterprise, but I will not need to pursue the matter further because I see the anxiety of the hon. member (Mr. Carvell) to switch off that subject. I do feel it is due to the completeness of the little incident we had, that I recall the comparison between the

Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Company, and say, the Manitoba and Southeastern Company. In the case of the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Company, the promoters bonded the road to build it, which they were entitled to do, and got the land grant for building it, which they were entitled to have. In the case of the Manitoba and Southeastern Company they did exactly the same thing. In the case though of the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan, the promoters retained the land grant and sold the road so bonded, as they were entitled to do.
Mr.' CAEVELL: To Mackenzie and Mann.

They sold it later on to Mackenzie and Mann. They sold the road so bonded and retained for themselves the land grant, and that is exactly what Mackenzie and Mann could have done in the case of the Manitoba and Southeastern. In the case of the Winnipeg and Hudson bay; in the case of the Lake Manitoba Eailway and Canal Company, they could have done exactly what the promoters did in the case of the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan, and no one could have criticised them for it, as no one could criticise the promoters of the Qu'Appelle Long Lake and Saskatchewan. What did these latter promoters do? They retained for themselves the land grant and consequently Mackenzie, Mann and Company could have retained for themselves the land grants in these other roads. The cases were on all fours all through their history. I only set out to show that Mackenzie, Mann and Company were entitled to these lands, and they were entitled to hold them and make title for them. They were in a position to sell them and they did so to the extent of 100,000 acres, and the rest of the land grant and the right to the land was transferred to the Canadian Northern. Who will say that that was not a transfer of the property of Mackenzie, Mann and Company to the Canadian Northern. If to-day the promoters of the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan railway were to take their land grant, if they own it, and transfer it to the Q.u'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan
would the hon. member for Carleton say they did not transfer any of their own property to that railroad; would he say they had never put a dollar in the enterprise? Would the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) say : hear, hear, when the hon. member (Mr. Carvell) uttered such words? I do not think so. We do not need to go any further on the matter of the land grant.
It has been brought in all week; hardly an hon, gentleman opposite spoke who did not assert, and reassert, and reiterate, that Mackenzie and Mann had never put a dollar in the road.
I never said so.

The hon. member for
South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) did not, and he is to be honoured for it. He knew better, but he heard those behind him say it.
Those behind him expressed the truth.

It will hardly be
argued that we have no security on the townsites which were the property of Mackenzie, Mann and Company as their own, but I do not wish to dilate on it at this late hour. It was not my desire to be controversial, and I know I was not ugly, but it was my desire to try and do some little fairness to the men who had done something for this road.
Amendment (Mr. Carvell) negatived.
On the motion of Mr. Pelletier that the committee report progress:
It is understood that the particular item we were on still stands.

Yes, subject to the loss of the amendment.
Progress reported.
